body:
Every humus application is a bedrock.App, and the root package’s humus.App is the lifecycle every humus service runs. It reads its settings, listens for signals, builds its telemetry and the user’s dependencies, runs one or more Services, drains and shuts them down within a grace period, releases what was built, shuts its telemetry down and turns the outcome into an exit status.
A service’s main is func main() { humus.Main(app.Init) }, where app.Init is the end user’s Init. humus.Main builds the humus.App from its defaults and that Init, applies the options it is given, and runs the App on the OS process. Options change the App’s fields, so everything this page says about humus.App is what Main runs. The runtime packages — REST, gRPC, jobs, queues — export Services for Init to return, not Apps, and one whose Services need a drain wraps Main with defaults of its own: see Runtime packages. An App that mixes runtimes, such as a REST API and a gRPC service in one process, needs nothing more.
Telemetry is part of the lifecycle: the App builds it before Init, logs through it, and shuts it down last. See Telemetry below, and the Telemetry page for what a service does with it. Health is a Service like any other: an App’s Init returns the health package’s Service next to its other Services, and Health explains what it does to readiness through the lifecycle.
The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: the humus App lifecycle and Proposal: humus.Main, with its revision 1 and revision 2. The telemetry integration is in Proposal: OpenTelemetry without globals, Revision 2.
Main humus.Main(init, opts...) runs an App on the OS process and exits the process with the App’s status. It never returns, and only init is required. This main passes the end user’s Init and one option, for its own telemetry:
humus.Main(Init, humus.WithTelemetry(buildTelemetry)) Main builds the App before it runs anything:
It starts from Main’s defaults for Host, Telemetry, ShutdownGracePeriod and Drain. It sets Init to init, so an option sees the end user’s Init and may wrap it, for example to add a Service next to the end user’s. It applies opts in order, so a later option wins over an earlier one. It is then bedrock.Main of that App, the only place a humus program touches the real process. It panics if init or one of opts is nil.
An option is a humus.Option, a func(*humus.App). humus has one for each field Main defaults:
Option Sets humus.WithHost(h) App.Host humus.WithTelemetry(b) App.Telemetry, the App’s telemetry.Builder humus.WithShutdownGracePeriod(d) App.ShutdownGracePeriod, the grace period when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD is not set humus.WithDrain(d) App.Drain, the drain when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY is not set. humus.WithDrain(nil) removes a drain that an earlier option set An option changes exported fields, so an end user or a runtime package can write one of their own as a function literal, and one option may set several fields.
buildTelemetry is the end user’s Builder. It starts from the telemetry package’s defaults, which write log records to standard output, and names the service:
func buildTelemetry(ctx context.Context, p bedrock.Process, dial telemetry.Dialer) (telemetry.SDK, error) { s := telemetry.DefaultSettings() s.ServiceName = "greeter" return telemetry.New(ctx, s, dial, p.Stdout) } A main that wants none of Main’s defaults can still write bedrock.Main(humus.App{…}), and sets every field itself:
bedrock.Main(humus.App{ Host: humus.OSHost(), ShutdownGracePeriod: 30 * time.Second, // when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD is not set Drain: humus.DrainDelay(5 * time.Second), // when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY is not set Telemetry: buildTelemetry, Init: Init, }) The defaults Field Main’s default Why Host humus.OSHost() Main runs only in main. A test runs its App with humustest.Start, which uses a test Host. Telemetry telemetry.New with telemetry.DefaultSettings(), the Host’s Dial and the Process’s stdout Logs go to stdout as JSON lines, and spans get real IDs without being exported. A service that exports anything passes its own Builder with humus.WithTelemetry. ShutdownGracePeriod 20s It fits inside Kubernetes’ default terminationGracePeriodSeconds of 30s, with telemetry’s 5s shutdown after it and a margin for the process to exit. Drain none Only a Service that a load balancer routes to, and that keeps serving until Shutdown, needs a drain, and the package that provides it sets one. The worst case from a signal to the exit is 20s of grace period and 5s of telemetry shutdown, telemetry.Settings.ShutdownTimeout: 25s, inside Kubernetes’ 30s. A drain comes out of the same budget, so a runtime package that sets one shortens its grace period to fit.
The defaults live in Main, not in App. humus.App’s fields keep their meaning: a zero ShutdownGracePeriod fails startup, and a nil Drain doesn’t wait. An operator overrides the grace period and the drain through their variables, whatever Main or an option set, without a rebuild.
Runtime packages A job, a queue consumer and the health Service stop on Serve’s context, so they run on humus.Main’s defaults and need no Main of their own. A runtime package whose Services need a drain, such as an HTTP or gRPC server that keeps serving until Shutdown, wraps Main instead:
It exports its defaults as one humus.Option, so that a test runs with them too. Its Main applies those defaults and then the end user’s options, and calls humus.Main. The end user’s options come last, so they win over the package’s. The HTTP server’s Main and defaults are httpserver.Main and httpserver.Defaults, with a 5s drain and a 10s grace period, which fit inside the 25s budget with telemetry’s 5s: Serving HTTP explains them. The gRPC server’s are grpcserver.Main and grpcserver.Defaults, with a 5s drain and a 15s grace period, which use the whole 25s budget with telemetry’s 5s: gRPC services explains them. The root package’s tests don’t import a runtime package, so the samples on this page use stand-ins of the same shape:
// httpDefaults stands in for a runtime package's defaults, such as // httpserver.Defaults: a 5s drain and a 10s grace period over humus.Main's. func httpDefaults() humus.Option { return func(a *humus.App) { a.Drain = humus.DrainDelay(5 * time.Second) a.ShutdownGracePeriod = 10 * time.Second } } // httpMain stands in for a runtime package's Main, such as httpserver.Main: // humus.Main with the package's defaults applied before the end user's // options, so that the end user's options win. func httpMain(init func(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error), opts ...humus.Option) { humus.Main(init, append([]humus.Option{httpDefaults()}, opts...)...) } The end user’s main calls the package’s Main, and its test passes the package’s defaults with humustest.WithApp(httpDefaults()), as Testing shows, or with the package’s own Start, such as httpservertest.Start or grpcservertest.Start:
httpMain(Init, humus.WithTelemetry(buildTelemetry)) A process picks its Main by what a load balancer routes to. It uses an HTTP or gRPC package’s Main when that server is one a load balancer routes to, as an API next to a job is. A job or a consumer next to a probes or metrics server stays on humus.Main: nothing routes to that server, and a drain would make a finished job wait for the whole delay.
In a mixed process, the package’s budget is everyone’s. A job or a consumer next to a server that is routed to runs on that server’s package’s Main, so its work in flight at a signal gets that package’s drain and grace period: a 5s drain and a 10s grace period on httpserver.Main’s defaults, and a 5s drain and a 15s grace period on grpcserver.Main’s, rather than humus.Main’s 20s grace period with no drain. An end user who needs more passes humus.WithShutdownGracePeriod after the package’s defaults. On httpserver.Main’s defaults that fits within the 25s budget up to a 15s grace period. grpcserver.Main’s defaults already use the whole 25s, so a longer grace period there needs terminationGracePeriodSeconds raised to match, as gRPC services describes. An HTTP and a gRPC server in one process use either package’s Main. Each package’s defaults set both the drain and the grace period, so passing the other package’s defaults as well replaces both: the last one wins.
App An App has five fields:
Field Required Meaning Host yes the network and filesystem the App runs on: humus.OSHost() under Main, and a Host the test controls in a test ShutdownGracePeriod yes, unless HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD is set the grace period when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD is not set: 20s under Main. It must be positive, so the zero value fails startup Drain no the drain when HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY is not set: a humus.Drain, such as humus.DrainDelay(5 * time.Second), that runs between shutdown starting and Shutdown being called on the Services, and whose context is done once every Serve has returned. A nil Drain, Main’s default, means no pause Telemetry yes the telemetry.Builder that builds the App’s telemetry: under Main, its default or the end user’s own Builder, and in tests also telemetry.NoopBuilder or the Builder of humustest’s recorder, humustest.Telemetry Init yes builds the App’s dependencies and returns the Services to run ShutdownGracePeriod and Drain are defaults: an operator overrides either through its variable without a rebuild. How long to drain and how long to allow for shutdown depend on what the App runs — a REST or gRPC App needs time for a load balancer to stop sending it connections, and a job does not — so Main has opinions about them, the runtime packages that need other ones set their own, and the App literal has none.
Service A Service is a long-running part of an App: an HTTP server, a gRPC server, a queue consumer or a job. It has two methods, Serve and Shutdown, and the App gives it two shutdown signals, at different times:
Serve’s context is done as soon as the App starts shutting down, before the drain. Shutdown is called after the drain, with the grace period as its context’s deadline. A Service may stop on the first, as a job, a queue consumer or the health Service does: the health Service turns not ready then, so a load balancer stops sending the App new traffic. Or it may keep serving until the second, as an HTTP or gRPC Service does, so that a load balancer still draining connections towards it is answered. This Service keeps serving until Shutdown:
type server struct { out io.Writer ready chan struct{} stopped chan struct{} } func newServer(out io.Writer) *server { return &server{ out: out, ready: make(chan struct{}), stopped: make(chan struct{}), } } func (s *server) Serve(ctx context.Context) error { _, err := fmt.Fprintln(s.out, "serve: serving") close(s.ready) if err != nil { return err } <-s.stopped return nil } func (s *server) Shutdown(ctx context.Context) error { close(s.stopped) _, err := fmt.Fprintln(s.out, "shutdown: stopped serving") return err } Closing ready tells the example that runs it when it is serving. Serve returns nil when Shutdown stopped it or when it finished on its own. Any Service returning from Serve ends the App, so a job is just a Service that returns, and an App is never partly up. Shutdown is called on every Service, including one whose Serve has already returned, so it must be safe to call then. If its context is done before the Service has stopped, Shutdown stops it at once and returns an error that wraps the context’s error.
The drain The drain is the pause between shutdown starting and Shutdown being called on the Services, so that load balancers stop sending the App new work before its servers stop. It is a function, humus.Drain, so that what it waits for is the end user’s choice, and so that it can stop waiting once nothing is left to drain: a func(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) error. App.Drain holds it. Main sets none, and a nil Drain means no pause.
It ends once every Serve has returned. Run calls the Drain after Serve’s context is done, when it hasn’t yet received every Serve’s result, with the Setup that Init was given. The Drain’s context is done once every Service’s Serve has returned, because nothing is left to drain. A Service that stops on Serve’s context returns at once or once its work in flight is done, and a Service that keeps serving until Shutdown doesn’t return until after the drain. So, for an App with a Drain set:
The App’s Services The drain lasts a job, finished on its own nothing: Run doesn’t call the Drain a job, finished on its own, next to the health Service nothing: Run calls the Drain, and its context is done at once a job, interrupted by a signal until the run returns, at most the Drain’s delay a queue consumer until its records in flight are done, at most the Drain’s delay an HTTP or gRPC server, with or without the health Service the Drain’s whole delay a job and an HTTP server the Drain’s whole delay, unless both return first On humus.Main’s defaults there is no Drain, so none of these drain. An Init that returns no Services ends the App without a drain too, because there is nothing to drain.
humus.DrainDelay(d) is the usual kind of drain. It waits d, or until its context is done, and returns nil either way. A runtime package that needs a drain sets one in its defaults, and an end user passes one with humus.WithDrain(humus.DrainDelay(5 * time.Second)). It doesn’t look at the shutdown’s cause: after a Service returned on its own, it still gives load balancers its delay to notice that the pod is no longer ready. It panics if d is negative.
A Drain returns nil when its context is done. A done context is how a Drain learns that nothing is left to drain, which is a normal end, not a failure: a Drain that returns ctx.Err() then fails the App, with drain: context canceled in the cause. Run may call a Drain whose context is done at once, as for a finished job next to the health Service, so a Drain checks its context before it acts. A Drain returns when it is done or when its context is done, whichever comes first.
The Drain is not bounded by the grace period. Run waits for it to return, and the grace period starts after it. A Drain that ignores its context holds the App up until a second signal, or Kubernetes’ SIGKILL, ends the process. Its context keeps the values of Run’s context but is not cancelled with it. An error it returns is logged at ERROR, joined into the App’s cause as drain: and the error, and exits 1, and Shutdown is still called on every Service.
A Drain of the end user’s own checks ShutdownCause before it waits on a load balancer. humus.ShutdownCause(ctx) says why the shutdown started: after a signal, it is the signal’s cause, and Kubernetes is terminating the pod and removing it from load balancers. When a Service returned on its own first, such as a job next to an API, it wraps humus.ErrServiceReturned, and nothing outside is draining the App. A Drain that waited for deregistration then would wait for something nothing triggers. This Drain polls a load balancer through s.Host.Dial, so that it runs on a test Host too, and only after a signal:
func deregisteringDrain(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) error { if errors.Is(humus.ShutdownCause(ctx), humus.ErrServiceReturned) { return nil // no signal came, so nothing is deregistering the pod } return waitUntilDeregistered(ctx, s.Host.Dial) } waitUntilDeregistered returns nil when ctx is done. The end user passes the Drain with humus.WithDrain:
humus.Main(Init, humus.WithDrain(deregisteringDrain)) The Drain gets the Setup, not what Init built, because it is chosen in main, before Init runs. Work at shutdown that needs Init’s dependencies, such as deregistering from service discovery, belongs in a Service that stops on Serve’s context: it sees shutdown start at the same moment, and the Drain then waits for whatever has to follow it.
HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY replaces any Drain. When it is set, Run uses humus.DrainDelay of its value in place of App.Drain, whatever that is, and adds a drain to an App that has none. An operator can always replace a Drain that misbehaves, from the same manifest that sets terminationGracePeriodSeconds. See Settings.
Host A Host is what humus hands an App beyond its process: Listen, Dial and a filesystem, FS. Every field is required. Under humus.Main an App runs on humus.OSHost(), which is net.Listen, a net.Dialer’s DialContext, and an FS that calls package os directly. In a test it runs on a Host whose listeners, dialler and filesystem the test controls, so that a whole App runs without touching the real host.
Host is meant for user code as well as for humus. Hand Host.Dial to a client that takes a dial function, such as pgx’s DialFunc, and open files through Host.FS rather than through package os.
Why FS hands out *os.File FS names files by OS path and opens them as *os.File, rather than through an in-memory filesystem:
Libraries that need a real file or a path keep working in a test: SQLite drivers, archive libraries, programs started with os/exec. There is no fake filesystem to build and keep in line with the real one. It is a one-way decision. An *os.File is always an OS handle, so moving to an in-memory filesystem later would change every signature. OSHost’s FS is not os.OpenRoot("/"), because an os.Root refuses to follow absolute symbolic links even when it is rooted at /, and paths on a real host routinely pass through them.
What it costs a test: the rule is that it opens no file outside its own temporary directory; it cannot make a write fail with a full disk, so code that needs that test puts an io.Writer seam in its own code; and file modification times are real under synctest, so code that compares ModTime() with time.Now() needs Chtimes in its tests.
Setup and OnStop Init is given a *humus.Setup holding the bedrock.Process the App is run with, the App’s Host and its telemetry, Setup.Telemetry. Init reads its configuration from Setup.Process, builds its dependencies on Setup.Host, takes their tracers, meters and loggers from Setup.Telemetry, and returns the Services to run. Its context is done when the App receives an interrupt or SIGTERM, so a slow Init, such as one retrying a database connection, is cancelled by a signal.
Setup.OnStop registers a function that releases something Init built. The functions work like t.Cleanup: they run in reverse order of registration once every Service has stopped, and they run when Init fails partway through too. So register each release as soon as the thing it releases is built:
func Init(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { out := s.Process.Stdout s.OnStop(func(context.Context) error { _, err := fmt.Fprintln(out, "on stop: close the cache") return err }) s.OnStop(func(context.Context) error { _, err := fmt.Fprintln(out, "on stop: close the queue") return err }) if _, err := config.Env(s.Process.Environment, "DATABASE_URL").Read(ctx); err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78: init: config DATABASE_URL: not found } return []humus.Service{newServer(out)}, nil } Run without DATABASE_URL, this App closes the queue and then the cache, logs init: config DATABASE_URL: not found at ERROR through its telemetry, and exits 78.
The OnStop functions share the grace period with the Services’ Shutdown: the context each is given is done when the grace period runs out.
What Run does, in order Reads the lifecycle’s settings from the process’s environment, defaulting each to its App field: under Main, that is Main’s default, or what an option set. A malformed one, or a bad default, exits 78 before the App listens for signals, and Init is never called. Listens for an interrupt and SIGTERM through the process’s NotifyContext, before the telemetry and Init, so a signal during a slow Builder or a slow Init cancels it. Builds the telemetry by calling App.Telemetry. If it fails, Init is never called, and the App exits 78 when a *config.Error is in the error chain, or 1 otherwise. Sets OpenTelemetry’s process-wide error handler, which writes each export error to standard error. Calls Init. If it fails, runs the OnStop functions registered so far, within the grace period, and exits 78 when a *config.Error is in Init’s error chain, or 1 otherwise. Calls Serve on every Service concurrently, and logs serving. Waits for a signal, or for the first Service to return. Stops listening for signals, so that a second interrupt or SIGTERM takes its default action and ends the process at once, cancels the context passed to Serve, and logs shutting down. When it hasn’t yet received every Serve’s result, calls the drain, with the Setup that Init was given: humus.DrainDelay of HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY when that is set, and App.Drain otherwise. Its context keeps the values of Run’s context but is not cancelled with it, is done once every Serve has returned, and gives humus.ShutdownCause why the shutdown started. Run collects the Serve results that arrive in the meantime and waits for the drain to return. A drain error is logged at ERROR and joined into the cause as drain: and the error. Calls Shutdown on every Service concurrently, waits for every Serve to return, and then runs the OnStop functions in reverse order of registration. All of this happens within one grace period, HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD, which starts after the drain. Then it logs stopped. Shuts the telemetry down. Returns the exit status. An Init that returns no Services, and a Service that returns on its own when it is the only one, end the App without calling the drain, as there is nothing to drain. A cancelled root context still gets a graceful shutdown: the grace period keeps the context’s values but not its cancellation. Every failure is the cause of the exit status. Once the telemetry is built, each failure is logged through it, one record per error; before that, it is written to standard error, one line per error. The lifecycle never recovers a panic.
Telemetry App.Telemetry is the App’s telemetry.Builder, and it is required. Main’s default calls telemetry.New with telemetry.DefaultSettings(), so log records go to standard output as JSON lines and nothing is exported. A service that exports anything passes its own Builder with humus.WithTelemetry, such as buildTelemetry above, which sources telemetry.Settings however it likes and calls telemetry.New. A test run with humustest.Start keeps Main’s default unless it passes telemetry.NoopBuilder, or the Builder of humustest’s recorder, humustest.Telemetry, when the test asserts on what the App emits. Telemetry explains how to write the Builder, what the defaults are, the console log format, and how logs get their trace context.
Telemetry is built after NotifyContext and before Init. Run calls App.Telemetry with the context that a signal cancels, the Process, and the Host’s Dial, so the OTLP exporters reach the collector through the Host. A Builder that runs a resource detector can be slow, because a cloud detector calls its metadata server, so a signal cancels it as it cancels a slow Init. A failure exits 78 when a *config.Error is in its chain, such as a malformed variable the Builder read, and 1 otherwise. A Builder that returns an SDK with a nil field fails too, and exits 1. In every case Init is never called. Init gets the SDK in Setup.Telemetry, and hands it on to its Services.
Failures are logged through telemetry. The lifecycle logs with the OpenTelemetry Logs API, through Setup.Telemetry.LoggerProvider.Logger("github.com/z5labs/humus"): its own records, serving, shutting down and stopped, at INFO, and every failure after the telemetry is built at ERROR, one record per error, so an operator sees them in the same log stream as everything else. humus has no logging bridge of its own. Standard error still gets what telemetry cannot report itself:
a failure to build telemetry, and a malformed lifecycle setting, which come before there is any telemetry; export errors, each on one line starting with telemetry: . Run sets OpenTelemetry’s process-wide error handler to write them there, because a failing exporter cannot report its own failure; a failure to shut telemetry down. Telemetry shuts down last: after the OnStop functions, or after a failed Init and its OnStop functions. So the spans and logs that record a slow or failed shutdown are still exported. Its context keeps the root context’s values but not its cancellation, and it is separate from the grace period: telemetry.New bounds it with Settings.ShutdownTimeout. A failure to shut telemetry down is joined into the cause of the exit status, and it turns an exit 0 into 1.
Settings Variable Default Meaning HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD App.ShutdownGracePeriod: Main’s 20s, unless an option sets another bounds the whole shutdown: every Service’s Shutdown and every OnStop function share it. A time.ParseDuration string, such as 30s, that must be positive. HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY App.Drain: none under Main, unless an option sets one the drain, in place of App.Drain, whatever that is, including none: humus.DrainDelay of a time.ParseDuration string, such as 5s, that must not be negative; 0s means no pause. These are the only variables the lifecycle reads, and the root package is the one place humus reads them. Each value is checked after its default, so a bad default fails the same way as a bad variable: an App whose ShutdownGracePeriod is zero, run without HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD, exits 78 with config HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD: must be positive. When both values are bad, both are reported, one line each.
Exit codes Code When Cause 0 a signal stopped the App and it shut down in time the signal 0 a Service returned nil on its own, and the App shut down in time none 1 (humus.ExitFailure) the telemetry could not be built, or its SDK has a nil field the error 1 (humus.ExitFailure) Init, a Service, a Service’s Shutdown, an OnStop function or the telemetry’s shutdown failed every error, joined 1 (humus.ExitFailure) the shutdown ran past the grace period a *humus.GracePeriodError 2 never set by humus: Go’s exit status for an unrecovered panic 78 (humus.ExitConfig) a setting is missing or malformed, including a config value read by the telemetry Builder or by Init a *config.Error in the chain 78 is EX_CONFIG from sysexits.h. It tells an operator “fix the configuration” apart from “the service failed”. Everything else that fails exits 1, and a test tells those failures apart by their cause: errors.AsType[*config.Error] for a config error, and errors.AsType[*humus.GracePeriodError] for a shutdown that ran out of time. A flag usage error is an Init failure and exits 1.
Testing a whole App An App runs whole inside a test. humustest.Start runs the App that Main would run for an Init, with Main’s defaults, on a test Host in place of humus.OSHost() and on a fake process from bedrocktest, whose arguments and environment the test sets, whose output the test reads, and to which the test sends fake signals. Options given with humustest.WithApp change the App as they would in main. testing/synctest runs it in fake time, so a five-second drain passes at once and is measured exactly. The lifecycle’s own tests run it with fake Services:
type fakeService struct { serve func(ctx context.Context) error shutdown func(ctx context.Context) error mu sync.Mutex shutdownCalls int } func (s *fakeService) Serve(ctx context.Context) error { if s.serve == nil { <-ctx.Done() return nil } return s.serve(ctx) } func (s *fakeService) Shutdown(ctx context.Context) error { s.mu.Lock() s.shutdownCalls++ s.mu.Unlock() if s.shutdown == nil { return nil } return s.shutdown(ctx) } This test runs an App with an HTTP-like Service and a consumer through a whole lifecycle, from SIGTERM to the OnStop functions, with a 5s drain:
func TestStart_a_whole_App(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { // api keeps serving until Shutdown, as an HTTP server does. stopped := make(chan struct{}) var shutdownAt time.Time api := &fakeService{ serve: func(context.Context) error { <-stopped return nil }, shutdown: func(context.Context) error { shutdownAt = time.Now() close(stopped) return nil }, } // consumer stops as soon as Serve's context is done, as a queue // consumer does. var consumerStoppedAt time.Time consumer := &fakeService{serve: func(ctx context.Context) error { <-ctx.Done() consumerStoppedAt = time.Now() return nil }} var poolClosedAt time.Time init := func(_ context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { s.OnStop(func(context.Context) error { poolClosedAt = time.Now() return nil }) return []humus.Service{api, consumer}, nil } p, status := humustest.Start(t, init, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithDrain(humus.DrainDelay(5*time.Second))), ) <-p.Notified(syscall.SIGTERM) synctest.Wait() // every Serve has started sigterm := time.Now() p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) st := <-status if st.Code() != 0 { t.Errorf("code = %d, want 0: %v", st.Code(), st.Cause()) } if !errors.Is(st.Cause(), context.Canceled) { t.Errorf("cause = %v, want the signal", st.Cause()) } if got := consumerStoppedAt.Sub(sigterm); got != 0 { t.Errorf("consumer stopped %s after SIGTERM, want at once", got) } if got := shutdownAt.Sub(sigterm); got != 5*time.Second { t.Errorf("Shutdown called %s after SIGTERM, want after the 5s drain", got) } if api.calls() != 1 || consumer.calls() != 1 { t.Errorf("Shutdown called %d and %d times, want once each", api.calls(), consumer.calls()) } if poolClosedAt.IsZero() || poolClosedAt.Before(shutdownAt) { t.Errorf("OnStop ran at %v, want it after Shutdown at %v", poolClosedAt, shutdownAt) } if got := p.Stderr(); got != "" { t.Errorf("stderr = %q, want nothing", got) } }) } synctest reports a deadlock when a goroutine the App started outlives the test body, which makes it a leak detector for Services. For an HTTP Service the cost is that handlers must honour r.Context(), because a handler that ignores it after the server force-closes the connection outlives the test.
Testing a humus App covers humustest.Start in full, and runs Apps that serve real HTTP, on a humustest Host whose network and filesystem the test controls.
Ambient leaks Some dependencies read the real process behind an App’s back, so they reach around the bedrock.Process and the Host an App is given, and a test can neither control nor see what they read. Avoid them, or configure them explicitly from Setup:
pgx reads the real process. pgx.ParseConfig and pgxpool.ParseConfig take every setting the connection string leaves out from PGHOST, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD and the other PG* variables of the real environment, and default the user to the OS user. They read the password file that PGPASSFILE names, or ~/.pgpass, from the real disk and use it when the connection string sets no password, and they pick up client certificates from ~/.postgresql. The config they return dials the real network: set cfg.ConnConfig.DialFunc = s.Host.Dial before opening the pool. Its LookupFunc still resolves host names with the real resolver. flag.CommandLine and flag.ExitOnError read os.Args and exit the process. Parse p.Args[1:] with a flag.FlagSet of your own, using flag.ContinueOnError. An exec.Cmd with a nil Env inherits the real environment. Build its Env from the keys you know, reading each through p.Environment. http.ProxyFromEnvironment, the Proxy of http.DefaultTransport, reads the proxy variables of the real environment, and http.DefaultClient dials the real network rather than through Host.Dial. crypto/x509’s system roots. A TLS config with no RootCAs verifies the server against the system’s roots, which crypto/x509 reads from the files and directories SSL_CERT_FILE and SSL_CERT_DIR name in the real environment, and from the OS’s certificate files on the real disk, not through the Host. An httpclient client whose Settings.TLS has no RootCAs reads them. A service that calls only its own services sets RootCAs to its CA, and a test sets it to the pool of a CA from humustest.NewCA, as Calling HTTP services describes. slog.Default writes to the real standard error unless it is replaced, and replacing it is process-wide state. OpenTelemetry’s process-wide error handler, which Run sets. In a process with several Apps, the last App to start gets every App’s export errors, so a test that asserts on export errors does not run in parallel. OpenTelemetry’s internal logger, which writes its own errors to the real standard error. OTEL_GO_X_*, OpenTelemetry’s experimental features, which the SDK reads from the real environment. Any resource detector the end user opts into in Settings.ResourceOptions, which reads the real host, such as /etc, /proc and cgroups, or dials a metadata server rather than through Host.Dial. grpc-go’s logger. Its grpclog package reads GRPC_GO_LOG_SEVERITY_LEVEL, GRPC_GO_LOG_VERBOSITY_LEVEL and GRPC_GO_LOG_FORMATTER, and its internal/envconfig package reads its other GRPC_* variables, from the real environment, and it writes to the real standard error. Replacing it means grpclog.SetLoggerV2, which is process-wide state, so grpcserver sets none: an end user who wants grpc-go’s logs in their telemetry sets the logger in main, as gRPC services describes. flag, exec.Cmd, http.ProxyFromEnvironment and slog.Default are on bedrock’s own list. A dependency found reading the real process belongs on this list.

body:
The httpserver package serves an http.Handler over TLS as a humus.Service. The end user’s Init sources its Settings, builds the Service with httpserver.NewService and returns it, and httpserver.Main runs it with the defaults an HTTP server behind a load balancer needs: a 5s drain and a 10s grace period. Its test package, httpservertest, runs the same App in a test, on the same defaults, with an HTTP/2 client.
The package is the server half of what rest.Run did before the reset, without the REST DSL. It exports no App, runs no health Service and serves no probes: httphealth answers them, as Health probes describes. The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: HTTP server foundation, with its revision 1 and revision 2.
A service The end user’s Init sources httpserver.Settings with config.Struct, as Configuring a humus service describes, builds the handler, and returns the Service that NewService builds from both:
// Init is the end user's Init: it sources the Settings, builds the Service // with NewService and returns it, with any other Service the process runs. func Init(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { d := httpserver.DefaultSettings() env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) } settings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) httpserver.Settings { return httpserver.Settings{ // No .Default: Addr and TLS are required, so an unset ADDR or // TLS_PEM_FILE fails as not found. Addr: r.Get(env("ADDR").Validate(httpserver.CheckAddr)), TLS: r.Get(env("TLS_PEM_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Parse(serverTLS).Validate(httpserver.CheckTLS)), HTTP2Only: r.Get(env("HTTP2_ONLY").Parse(strconv.ParseBool).Default(d.HTTP2Only)), ReadHeaderTimeout: r.Get(env("READ_HEADER_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(d.ReadHeaderTimeout).Validate(httpserver.CheckReadHeaderTimeout)), ReadTimeout: r.Get(env("READ_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(d.ReadTimeout).Validate(httpserver.CheckReadTimeout)), WriteTimeout: r.Get(env("WRITE_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(d.WriteTimeout).Validate(httpserver.CheckWriteTimeout)), IdleTimeout: r.Get(env("IDLE_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(d.IdleTimeout).Validate(httpserver.CheckIdleTimeout)), MaxHeaderBytes: r.Get(env("MAX_HEADER_BYTES").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(d.MaxHeaderBytes).Validate(httpserver.CheckMaxHeaderBytes)), } }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78, naming every bad variable } mux := http.NewServeMux() mux.HandleFunc("GET /hello", greet) svc, err := httpserver.NewService(s, settings, mux) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{svc}, nil } The variable names are the service’s own: humus defines none of them. readFile and serverTLS are the end user’s helpers too, shown under TLS.
The service’s main is one call to httpserver.Main, here with a telemetry Builder that names the service, as Telemetry describes:
httpserver.Main(Init, humus.WithTelemetry(buildTelemetry)) NewService runs every check on the Settings again, rejects a nil handler, and then listens on Settings.Addr through the Setup’s Host, in Init. So a port that is already taken fails Init, and the App exits 1, and a connection that arrives before Serve runs waits in the backlog rather than being refused. The listener’s close is registered with s.OnStop, so an Init that fails after NewService still closes it. An Addr with port 0 listens on a free port, which Service.Addr reports.
Init returns the HTTP Service along with any other Service the process runs, such as a job or a queue consumer next to the API, or the health Service. Any Service returning ends the App.
Settings httpserver.Settings follows the settings convention: plain Go values, a DefaultSettings(), and a check for each field with a valid range. The package reads no environment variable and defines no variable name.
Field Default Valid Check Addr none: required host:port, with a port from 0 to 65535 CheckAddr TLS none: required a config that has a certificate and that HTTP/2 can use CheckTLS HTTP2Only false either none ReadHeaderTimeout 2s not negative CheckReadHeaderTimeout ReadTimeout 5s not negative CheckReadTimeout WriteTimeout 10s not negative CheckWriteTimeout IdleTimeout 120s not negative CheckIdleTimeout MaxHeaderBytes 1 << 20, 1 MiB positive CheckMaxHeaderBytes The timeouts keep net/http’s meaning of zero. A zero ReadTimeout or WriteTimeout means no timeout, and a zero ReadHeaderTimeout or IdleTimeout means ReadTimeout applies, so their checks accept zero. MaxHeaderBytes must be positive. In net/http a zero means 1 MiB, a default applied to a zero value, so CheckMaxHeaderBytes rejects it rather than letting zero mean something other than zero. HTTP2Only has no check, since both values are valid. See Protocols. Addr and TLS are required. DefaultSettings() leaves Addr "" and TLS nil, which CheckAddr and CheckTLS reject, so humus imposes no port and no certificate. The end user’s chains for them have no .Default, as in Init above, so a variable that isn’t set fails as not found. The App exits 78, and config.Struct names every variable at fault in one error. With neither set:
init: config ADDR: not found config TLS_PEM_FILE: not found NewService runs the same checks itself, so a Settings built in code with a bad field fails Init too, naming the field, such as Settings.TLS must not be nil. That error is no *config.Error, so the App exits 1: the fault is in the code, not in the configuration. How a bad value fails explains the exit codes.
TLS TLS is required. The Service serves HTTPS with Settings.TLS and nothing in plain text. There is no plain-HTTP setting and no self-signed fallback: a service that hasn’t sourced a certificate doesn’t start, rather than starting and failing every request.
The certificate The end user decodes the certificate from a file, read through s.Host.FS so that a test reads it from its own directory and production from the real disk, as Reading a file describes. How the certificate is stored and encoded is the end user’s decision. Init above reads one PEM file that holds the certificate chain and the private key:
// readFile returns a parser for config.Value.Parse that reads the whole // file a variable names, through fsys. func readFile(fsys humus.FS) func(name string) ([]byte, error) { return func(name string) ([]byte, error) { f, err := fsys.Open(name) if err != nil { return nil, err } defer func() { _ = f.Close() }() return io.ReadAll(f) } } // serverTLS returns a server's TLS config for a PEM file that holds its // certificate chain and its private key. func serverTLS(pem []byte) (*tls.Config, error) { cert, err := tls.X509KeyPair(pem, pem) if err != nil { return nil, err } return &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert}}, nil } A PKCS#12 bundle needs a password as well. This chain reads the bundle from the file TLS_PKCS12_FILE names, and decodes it with the password in TLS_PKCS12_PASSWORD, so a missing file, a missing password and a wrong one each fail as a config error with exit 78:
settings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) httpserver.Settings { settings := httpserver.DefaultSettings() settings.Addr = r.Get(env("ADDR").Validate(httpserver.CheckAddr)) settings.TLS = r.Get(env("TLS_PKCS12_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).FlatMap(func(bundle []byte) config.Value[*tls.Config] { return env("TLS_PKCS12_PASSWORD").Parse(pkcs12TLS(bundle)) }).Validate(httpserver.CheckTLS)) return settings }).Read(ctx) pkcs12TLS decodes the bundle with go-pkcs12, which humus doesn’t depend on:
// pkcs12TLS returns a parser for config.Value.Parse that decodes bundle, // a PKCS#12 bundle, with the password it is given, into a server's TLS // config. func pkcs12TLS(bundle []byte) func(password string) (*tls.Config, error) { return func(password string) (*tls.Config, error) { key, leaf, chain, err := pkcs12.DecodeChain(bundle, password) if err != nil { return nil, err } cert := tls.Certificate{Certificate: [][]byte{leaf.Raw}, PrivateKey: key, Leaf: leaf} for _, c := range chain { cert.Certificate = append(cert.Certificate, c.Raw) } return &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert}}, nil } } A certificate that rotates on disk, or one from autocert, is served from a config that sets GetCertificate instead of Certificates.
What CheckTLS rejects CheckTLS fails startup on a config that would otherwise fail only once Serve runs, or on every HTTP/2 connection. It rejects:
nil, which is what DefaultSettings() leaves TLS; a config with no certificate: none of Certificates, GetCertificate and GetConfigForClient set, which ServeTLS would reject with an error about a file named ""; a MaxVersion below TLS 1.2, with which Go’s HTTP/2 server refuses every connection with INADEQUATE_SECURITY, as RFC 9113 requires; CipherSuites that HTTP/2 can’t use: a list that has neither TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 nor TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, with a MinVersion below TLS 1.3. It accepts a config with only GetCertificate set, and CipherSuites without those two suites when MinVersion is TLS 1.3, which ignores CipherSuites. Like every check, its error doesn’t name the field: the chain that sourced the config names its variable.
Behind a proxy Traffic is encrypted all the way to the pod, whatever sits in front of it. So a load balancer, an ingress controller or a mesh sidecar in front of the pod connects to it over TLS: an AWS ALB target group’s protocol is HTTPS, and an ingress controller is told that its backend speaks HTTPS, such as ingress-nginx with its nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "HTTPS" annotation. That holds behind a mesh that already encrypts between pods too: every service needs a certificate. Whether the proxy verifies the pod’s certificate, and against which CA, is the proxy’s configuration.
A proxy that connects in plain HTTP gets a 400 Bad Request and the Service logs a TLS handshake error, as Telemetry shows.
Protocols HTTP/2 is always on and preferred. Every client that offers HTTP/2 in ALPN gets it, and a client that doesn’t falls back to HTTP/1.1. The Service sets http.Server.Protocols itself, so HTTP/2 doesn’t depend on net/http’s defaults or on the config’s NextProtos. GODEBUG=http2server=0 still turns HTTP/2 off in net/http, whatever the Service sets: that is an operator overriding Go, and the Service doesn’t second-guess it.
The ALPN order The Service serves a clone of Settings.TLS, so the end user’s config is never changed, and sets the clone’s ALPN protocols in this order:
h2; http/1.1, unless HTTP2Only is set; every other protocol the config’s NextProtos lists, in its order. The server’s order wins in ALPN. net/http on its own adds h2 and http/1.1 after whatever a config already lists, so a config that listed http/1.1 would prefer HTTP/1.1. The Service puts h2 first whatever the config lists. A protocol other than these two, such as autocert’s acme-tls/1, is still offered, after them: a client that offers only acme-tls/1 gets it, and one that offers acme-tls/1 and h2 gets h2.
HTTP2Only With Settings.HTTP2Only, the Service serves HTTP/2 alone. A client that offers only HTTP/1.1, or no ALPN at all, completes the TLS handshake and is then disconnected before a request is read: it sees its connection closed with no response, and the Service logs nothing.
It is off by default because that failure is silent, and some clients speak only HTTP/1.1:
an AWS ALB target group on its default protocol version, HTTP1; a Go client with its own Transport that sets a TLSClientConfig or a dialer of its own, and sets neither ForceAttemptHTTP2 nor Protocols. Such a Transport negotiates only HTTP/1.1. It is a Settings field, so an operator turns it on from the manifest, with HTTP2_ONLY=true in Init above, once every client speaks HTTP/2.
No h2c TLS is required, so there is no plain text to serve unencrypted HTTP/2 (h2c) on, and no setting for it. A client that sends h2c with prior knowledge gets no response, and the Service logs a TLS handshake error.
Shutdown The Service follows the two shutdown signals of a humus App:
Serve’s context being done changes nothing. It is done as soon as the App starts shutting down, and the Service keeps serving through the App’s drain, while load balancers stop sending it traffic. A request that arrives during the drain is served, and an in-flight request finishes. Shutdown stops accepting connections, closes idle ones and waits for in-flight requests, within the grace period. When the grace period runs out first, it calls Close, which closes every connection and so cancels the context of each request still in flight. The App then exits 1 with a *humus.GracePeriodError. Request contexts A request’s context, r.Context(), doesn’t derive from Serve’s context, which is done as soon as shutdown starts, so a request that arrives during the drain is still served. It is done when the client goes away, or when Close closes its connection at the end of the grace period.
A handler returns once r.Context() is done. One that ignores it outlives the App once its connection is closed: the process exits under it. In a test that runs the App inside testing/synctest, synctest reports its goroutine as a leak, still blocked when the test ends, which is how the end user’s tests find such a handler. A connection a handler hijacks, such as a WebSocket, isn’t tracked by Shutdown or by Close: the handler closes it itself.
The defaults httpserver.Main is humus.Main with httpserver.Defaults() applied before the end user’s options, and does nothing else. Defaults is one humus.Option that sets two of humus.Main’s defaults, and leaves the Host and the telemetry Builder as humus.Main’s:
A drain of humus.DrainDelay(5 * time.Second). Kubernetes removes a terminating pod from a Service’s endpoints asynchronously, so for a while after SIGTERM, load balancers still route requests to the pod. The Service keeps serving through the drain, so those requests are answered rather than refused. It keeps serving until Shutdown, so its Serve doesn’t return during the drain, and the drain lasts the whole 5s. A grace period of 10s, rather than humus.Main’s 20s, so that the drain fits in the same budget. From SIGTERM, then: the Service serves through the 5s drain; Shutdown then waits up to 10s for in-flight requests and closes what is left; and the telemetry’s shutdown, telemetry.Settings.ShutdownTimeout, takes up to 5s more. The worst case is 20s, inside the 25s that humus.Main budgets within Kubernetes’ default terminationGracePeriodSeconds of 30s. A service whose requests all finish during the drain exits 5s after SIGTERM, when the drain ends.
Overriding them The end user’s options come after Defaults, so they win. httpserver.Main(Init, humus.WithShutdownGracePeriod(15*time.Second)) has a 15s grace period and still the 5s drain, and humus.WithDrain(nil) removes the drain.
An operator overrides both without a rebuild, with the lifecycle’s variables: HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD sets the grace period, and HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY replaces the drain with a delay of its value, whatever Defaults or an option set. Each leaves the other as it was: with HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY=1s alone, the drain is 1s and the grace period still 10s.
terminationGracePeriodSeconds When Kubernetes stops a pod, it sends the container SIGTERM, and then SIGKILL once terminationGracePeriodSeconds have passed, 30 by default. A service that raises its drain or its grace period raises terminationGracePeriodSeconds with them, in the same manifest, to at least the drain, the grace period and the telemetry’s shutdown, plus a margin for the process to exit. Otherwise SIGKILL ends it first: its container exits 137, its OnStop functions never run, and the telemetry it had not yet exported is lost.
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: greeter spec: selector: matchLabels: app: greeter template: metadata: labels: app: greeter spec: # 10s drain + 20s grace period + 5s telemetry shutdown, and a margin. terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40 containers: - name: greeter image: registry.example.com/greeter:1.0.0 ports: - name: https containerPort: 8443 env: - name: ADDR value: ":8443" - name: TLS_PEM_FILE value: /etc/greeter/tls/tls.pem - name: HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY value: 10s - name: HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD value: 20s volumeMounts: - name: tls mountPath: /etc/greeter/tls readOnly: true volumes: - name: tls secret: secretName: greeter-tls # tls.pem: the certificate chain and the private key The drain does the job of a preStop hook that sleeps, which services without one add for the same reason. A pod that has both spends the hook’s sleep and the drain out of the same terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
httpserver.Main or humus.Main Which Main a process calls depends on what a load balancer routes to, as the lifecycle’s runtime packages explains:
A process uses httpserver.Main when a load balancer routes to its HTTP server, an API alone or an API next to a job or a consumer. The other Services then get the HTTP server’s drain and grace period, 15s in all, rather than humus.Main’s 20s. A process whose only HTTP server serves probes or metrics calls humus.Main, with no drain. Nothing routes to that server, and a drain would make a finished job wait for the whole delay. Health probes An API answers its probes on its own port. The end user’s Init mounts httphealth.NewHandler at "/health/" of the mux the Service serves, without http.StripPrefix, and returns the health Service whose Probes it answers from next to the HTTP Service:
mux := http.NewServeMux() mux.Handle("/", api) mux.Handle("/health/", httphealth.NewHandler(s, hs.Probes())) svc, err := httpserver.NewService(s, settings, mux) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{svc, hs}, nil The handler answers GET /health/liveness and GET /health/readiness with 200 or 503, and the kubelet probes them on the API’s port with scheme: HTTPS. It doesn’t verify the Service’s certificate:
readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /health/readiness port: 8443 # the API's port scheme: HTTPS An API that requires client certificates can’t be probed on its own port, since the kubelet presents none. It serves its probes with httphealth.NewService on a port of its own, over HTTPS, which owns the App’s readiness, so Init returns it next to the HTTP Service and no health Service. Health shows both wirings, the answers, the manifests and how to test them.
Telemetry The Service takes everything from the Setup’s telemetry, and never reads or sets OpenTelemetry’s globals. The handler is served wrapped in OpenTelemetry’s net/http instrumentation, otelhttp, given the TracerProvider, the MeterProvider and the Propagator of s.Telemetry.
The span and the metrics Each request gets one server span. Its parent is the trace context the request brought in, extracted with the Setup’s propagator, so a request joins its caller’s trace. The propagator comes from the telemetry Builder and decides which headers carry the trace context: the W3C traceparent and tracestate headers, and baggage, with telemetry.New’s.
The span is named after the method and the route pattern, such as GET /hello/{name}, when the handler sets Request.Pattern, as an http.ServeMux does. Otherwise it is named after the method alone, such as GET. That is otelhttp’s default name, which follows OpenTelemetry’s semantic conventions.
Each request also records OpenTelemetry’s HTTP server metrics, such as http.server.request.duration, on the Setup’s MeterProvider.
The log records The Service logs through the LoggerProvider of the Setup’s telemetry, with the OpenTelemetry Logs API and the logger name github.com/z5labs/humus/httpserver, which is the records’ instrumentation scope:
Record Severity When listening, with server.address set to Service.Addr INFO Serve starts each line net/http writes to the server’s error log, such as http: TLS handshake error from 10.0.0.7:51234: EOF ERROR net/http reports a failure, such as a TLS handshake error or a failure to accept a connection handler panicked, with exception.type, exception.message and exception.stacktrace, in the request’s context ERROR a handler panics: see Panics The lifecycle’s own records, such as serving and shutting down, come from the App as for any Service.
ErrorLog never reaches standard error. The Service sets the http.Server’s ErrorLog to a logger whose every line is an ERROR record. Without it, net/http would write to the log package’s default logger, which is the real standard error, outside the App’s telemetry.
TLS handshake errors from TCP health checks A load balancer or a probe that checks the port with TCP, such as a Kubernetes tcpSocket probe or a network load balancer’s TCP health check, opens a connection and closes it without a TLS handshake. net/http reports each one as a handshake error, so every check emits an ERROR record such as:
http: TLS handshake error from 10.0.0.7:51234: EOF The Service logs every line at ERROR rather than telling these apart, because telling them apart means matching net/http’s message text, which isn’t API. A team bothered by the noise filters it in its log pipeline, where a change in Go’s wording is a filter to update rather than a release of humus. With the OpenTelemetry Collector’s filter processor, for example:
processors: filter/tcp-health-checks: error_mode: ignore logs: log_record: - instrumentation_scope.name == "github.com/z5labs/humus/httpserver" and IsMatch(body, "^http: TLS handshake error from .*: EOF$") Matching on the scope as well as the text drops only the Service’s own records. A probe that checks the port with an HTTPS request, such as an httpGet probe with scheme: HTTPS, causes no handshake error.
Panics A handler that panics aborts its request, which is recorded but isn’t answered. The Service recovers the panic and:
records it on the request’s span as an exception event, with its type, message and stack trace, and sets the span’s status to Error; emits one ERROR record, handler panicked, with the same attributes, in the request’s context, so the record carries the span’s trace and span IDs; panics again with http.ErrAbortHandler, so net/http aborts the response without logging it a second time. No 500 is written, and no header the handler hadn’t written. Over HTTP/2 the client sees its stream reset, and over HTTP/1.1 its connection closed, even when the handler had already written part of its response. A 500 would turn a bug into an ordinary error response, counted with every other 5xx. Nothing reaches standard error, and the Service keeps serving every other request.
A protocol that defines an error response, such as REST, recovers in its own handler and writes that response itself, before the Service sees the panic. A handler that wants to abort a response without it being logged or recorded panics with http.ErrAbortHandler itself, which the Service passes through untouched.
Testing An HTTP service is tested whole, inside testing/synctest, as Testing a humus App describes for any App, with two functions from httpservertest:
httpservertest.Start is humustest.Start with httpserver.Defaults() applied before the test’s options, and does nothing else. A test of a main that calls httpserver.Main runs with the drain and the grace period production runs with, and can’t forget them. The test passes its Host, its telemetry and its environment as it would to humustest.Start, and options given with humustest.WithApp come after the defaults, so they win. httpservertest.NewClient(h, roots) returns h.HTTPClient() with a TLS config that trusts only roots, and a Transport whose Protocols is HTTP/2 alone. Every request it makes is HTTP/2, so a Service that stopped offering h2 fails the test rather than falling back to HTTP/1.1 unnoticed. Like h.HTTPClient(), it keeps keep-alives off. A whole service This test runs a handler on the package’s defaults, over HTTP/2, with a certificate from a CA that humustest.NewCA generates for the test, so no key or certificate is ever written into the repository. serves is a helper of the test file that returns an Init whose only Service serves the handler on DefaultSettings() on :8443, over TLS with the certificate:
func TestMain_serves_HTTP2_and_records_the_span(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { ca := humustest.NewCA(t) h := humustest.NewHost(t) tel := humustest.NewTelemetry() mux := http.NewServeMux() mux.HandleFunc("GET /hello/{name}", greet) p, status := httpservertest.Start(t, serves(ca.Issue(t, "localhost"), mux), humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host()), humus.WithTelemetry(tel.Builder())), ) <-h.Listening("localhost:8443") resp, err := httpservertest.NewClient(h, ca.Pool()).Get("https://localhost:8443/hello/humus") require.NoError(t, err) body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body) require.NoError(t, err) require.NoError(t, resp.Body.Close()) require.Equal(t, 2, resp.ProtoMajor) require.Equal(t, "hello, humus", string(body)) <-p.Notified(syscall.SIGTERM) p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) st := <-status require.Zero(t, st.Code(), "cause: %v", st.Cause()) spans := tel.Spans() require.Len(t, spans, 1) require.Equal(t, "GET /hello/{name}", spans[0].Name()) require.Empty(t, p.Stderr()) }) } Fake time means the drain costs the test nothing: the App exits 5s after SIGTERM, in no real time at all. A handler blocked on r.Context() sees it cancelled 15s after SIGTERM, once the drain and the grace period are both up, or 7s after with humustest.WithApp(humus.WithShutdownGracePeriod(2*time.Second)).
Giving the App its certificate Start makes no CA and no certificate: how the end user’s Init sources its certificate, from which variable and in which encoding, is the end user’s decision. The test gives it one the way production does. It issues a certificate from its CA, writes it into the Host’s filesystem with humustest.WithFiles, and sets the variables that name the file, and any password, with humustest.WithEnv. For an Init that reads the PKCS#12 bundle above:
ca := humustest.NewCA(t) bundle, password := ca.Issue(t, "localhost").PKCS12(t) h := humustest.NewHost(t, humustest.WithFiles(map[string][]byte{"tls.p12": bundle})) p, status := httpservertest.Start(t, InitPKCS12, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host()), humus.WithTelemetry(telemetry.NoopBuilder)), humustest.WithEnv(map[string]string{ "ADDR": ":8443", "TLS_PKCS12_FILE": "tls.p12", "TLS_PKCS12_PASSWORD": password, }), ) <-h.Listening("localhost:8443") Each certificate has a new random key, and each bundle a new random password, so nothing secret is fixed in the test. A test that builds the httpserver.Settings itself, as serves does, sets their TLS config from cert.TLS() instead. Either way, the test passes the CA’s Pool() to NewClient.
The same Init with no environment at all checks that Addr and TLS are required:
func TestInit_without_an_address_or_a_certificate_exits_78(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { _, status := httpservertest.Start(t, Init) st := <-status require.Equal(t, humus.ExitConfig, st.Code()) require.ErrorContains(t, st.Cause(), "config ADDR: not found") require.ErrorContains(t, st.Cause(), "config TLS_PEM_FILE: not found") }) } An HTTP/1.1 client A test that needs HTTP/1.1, to check the fallback or HTTP2Only, configures h.HTTPClient() itself: it trusts the CA, offers http/1.1 in ALPN, and sets the Transport’s Protocols. httpserver’s own tests do it with a helper:
// protocols is what a client offers in ALPN. type protocols struct{ http1, http2 bool } var ( offersH2 = protocols{http2: true} offersHTTP1 = protocols{http1: true} offersBoth = protocols{http1: true, http2: true} ) // client returns h's HTTP client, trusting only ca, and offering p. func client(h *humustest.Host, ca *humustest.CA, p protocols) *http.Client { c := h.HTTPClient() tr := c.Transport.(*http.Transport) tr.TLSClientConfig = &tls.Config{RootCAs: ca.Pool()} if !p.http2 { tr.TLSClientConfig.NextProtos = []string{"http/1.1"} } var protos http.Protocols protos.SetHTTP1(p.http1) protos.SetHTTP2(p.http2) tr.Protocols = &protos return c } NewClient works without httpservertest.Start. It needs only the Host the App runs on and the roots its certificate chains to, so it works next to an App started with humustest.Start, or with another runtime package’s Start, in a test of a process that serves HTTP next to another protocol.
The Service contract httpserver’s own tests hold the Service to the Service contract with humustest.TestService, and a Service of the end user’s own that wraps it is checked the same way:
func TestService_meets_the_Service_contract(t *testing.T) { humustest.TestService(t, func(t *testing.T, s *humus.Setup) humus.Service { settings := httpserver.DefaultSettings() settings.Addr = ":8443" cert := humustest.NewCA(t).Issue(t, "localhost") settings.TLS = &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert.TLS()}} svc, err := httpserver.NewService(s, settings, http.NotFoundHandler()) require.NoError(t, err) return svc }) } The Service keeps serving after Serve’s context is done, so the subtest for Shutdown after Serve has returned on its own reports SKIP, as TestService documents.
Migration from rest.Run httpserver replaces the server half of rest.Run from before the reset. Its REST half moves to Proposal: REST endpoint DSL and OpenAPI, in wave 4 of the charter.
Before the reset With httpserver rest.Run(ctx, opts...), its server half httpserver.Main(Init, opts...), with the end user’s Init returning the Service from httpserver.NewService internal/httpserver.App httpserver.Service rest.Port(...), HUMUS_REST_PORT=8443 Settings.Addr, required, sourced from whatever variable the end user names rest.ReadTimeout, ReadHeaderTimeout, WriteTimeout, IdleTimeout, MaxHeaderBytes and their HUMUS_REST_* variables the Settings fields of the same names, with the same defaults rest.TLSConfig(...), HUMUS_REST_TLS_PKCS12_FILE and _PASSWORD Settings.TLS, required, a *tls.Config the end user decodes from a file read through s.Host.FS. PKCS#12 decoding is the end user’s, with go-pkcs12 if they like. a self-signed certificate when no TLS is configured exit 78 when the end user’s certificate variable isn’t set; a config with no certificate, or one HTTP/2 can’t use, fails CheckTLS whatever bedrock’s HTTP runtime and net/http’s defaults negotiated HTTP/2 always on and first in ALPN, with HTTP/1.1 as a fallback that Settings.HTTP2Only turns off otelhttp.NewHandler(h, "rest") on the globals the Service’s instrumentation, with s.Telemetry’s providers and propagator, and spans named after the route Shutdown(context.Background()) Shutdown bounded by the grace period, then Close RecoverPanics around the runtime no recovery in the lifecycle; a handler’s panic aborts its request, recorded in telemetry net/http’s error log on the real stderr ERROR records through the App’s telemetry
