title: Serving HTTP

body:
The httpclient package calls another service over HTTP. httpclient.NewClient builds a client for one dependency in the end user’s Init, from Settings the end user sources, and returns a plain *http.Client. Its calls go through the Setup’s Host, are traced and measured with the Setup’s telemetry, are retried when that is safe, and fail at once while a circuit breaker says the dependency keeps failing.
Service code, generated clients and SDKs take the *http.Client as they take any other, and depend on net/http’s type rather than on this package, so a unit test of that code passes any client. The client dials only through the Setup’s Host, so a test runs the end user’s whole App, its outbound calls included, on humustest’s network, as Testing shows.
The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: outbound HTTP clients, with its revision 1.
A client for each dependency The end user’s Init sources the dependency’s httpclient.Settings, builds its client with NewClient, and hands the client to the code that calls the dependency, here the handler of an httpserver Service:
// Init is the end user's Init: it sources the payments dependency's // Settings, builds its client with NewClient, and hands the client to the // handler of an httpserver Service. func Init(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { d := httpclient.DefaultSettings() env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) } paymentsSettings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) httpclient.Settings { c := d // No .Default: BaseURL is required, and the dependency is https, // so PAYMENTS_CA_FILE is too. c.BaseURL = r.Get(env("PAYMENTS_URL").Parse(url.Parse).Validate(httpclient.CheckBaseURL)) c.TLS = r.Get(env("PAYMENTS_CA_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Parse(trusting).Validate(httpclient.CheckTLS)) c.Timeout = r.Get(env("PAYMENTS_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(d.Timeout).Validate(httpclient.CheckTimeout)) return c }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78, naming every bad variable } serverSettings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) httpserver.Settings { c := httpserver.DefaultSettings() c.Addr = r.Get(env("ADDR").Validate(httpserver.CheckAddr)) c.TLS = r.Get(env("TLS_PEM_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Parse(serverTLS).Validate(httpserver.CheckTLS)) return c }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err } // One client for the dependency, built once and shared by every // request the handler serves. payments, err := httpclient.NewClient(s, paymentsSettings) if err != nil { return nil, err } api := newAPI(payments, paymentsSettings.BaseURL) svc, err := httpserver.NewService(s, serverSettings, api) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{svc}, nil } The handler joins its paths onto the BaseURL, and passes its request’s context to the call, so the call ends when the request does:
mux.HandleFunc("GET /orders/{id}/payment", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { // The call ends with the request's context, and service code joins // its paths onto the BaseURL. u := base.JoinPath("charges", r.PathValue("id")) req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(r.Context(), http.MethodGet, u.String(), nil) if err != nil { http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusInternalServerError) return } resp, err := payments.Do(req) if err != nil { http.Error(w, "payments is unavailable", http.StatusBadGateway) return } defer func() { _ = resp.Body.Close() }() if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK { http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("payments answered %d", resp.StatusCode), http.StatusBadGateway) return } _, _ = io.Copy(w, resp.Body) }) The service’s main is the server’s, as Serving HTTP describes:
httpserver.Main(Init, humus.WithTelemetry(buildTelemetry)) A client is not a humus.Service. NewClient opens no connection, and Init returns no Service for it. It registers one function with s.OnStop, which closes the client’s idle connections once every Service has stopped, so nothing is still calling the dependency by then. It runs when Init fails after NewClient too. A call in flight ends with its own context: a handler’s call ends when its request’s context does, so the client has nothing to drain.
One client per dependency A dependency is an origin: the scheme, host and port of Settings.BaseURL, with the scheme’s default port when the URL has none, so https://payments and https://payments:443 are one origin. The client sends requests to that origin and to no other. A request to another origin fails without being sent, and nothing is dialled, with an error such as:
httpclient: request to https://ledger:8443 on a client for https://payments:8443 BaseURL’s path, if it has one, is for service code to join request paths onto. The client doesn’t use it. A redirect within the origin is followed, up to 10, as net/http’s default policy does; a redirect to another origin isn’t, and service code gets the 3xx response, whose Location header it may read.
Build each client once, in Init, and share it between every Service that calls the dependency. That is why NewClient takes the *humus.Setup. The cost that matters is a client built for each call: it pools nothing, so every call dials and handshakes, and each one registers one more function with s.OnStop.
Two clients of one origin Two APIs behind one gateway, which the end user wants configured separately, get two clients of one origin, each with its own BaseURL path and its own Settings, and so each with its own breaker and retry budget:
// Two clients of one origin, each with its own Settings, built // once in Init and shared by everything that calls them. payments, err := httpclient.NewClient(s, paymentsSettings) if err != nil { return nil, err } ledger, err := httpclient.NewClient(s, ledgerSettings) if err != nil { return nil, err } Why pooling costs nothing A client per dependency pools connections as one shared http.Transport would, since net/http keys its idle connections by scheme, host and port, and a shared transport never lends one dependency’s connection to another. The two differ in two ways, and neither is a cost in practice:
Idle limits are per client. Each client keeps up to 100 idle connections to its origin for 90s, where one shared transport’s MaxIdleConns would cap every dependency together. A process with many dependencies can hold more idle sockets, up to what each dependency’s busiest burst opened, until they have been idle for 90s. In return, a burst to one dependency never evicts another’s idle connections, which would cost each a new TLS handshake. net/http’s default of 2 idle connections per host would make a busy client open and close connections on every burst. Two clients of one origin don’t share connections. Each opens its own, which over HTTP/2 is one more connection for each client. Settings httpclient.Settings follows the settings convention: plain Go values, a DefaultSettings(), and a check for each field with a valid range. The package reads no environment variable and defines no variable name: the end user’s Init sources each field with config.Struct, with whatever variable names the service uses, and passes the field’s check to Validate, as Init above does. An operator’s bad value then fails startup with exit 78, naming the variable.
Field Default Valid Check BaseURL none: required an absolute http or https URL with a host, and no user info, query or fragment CheckBaseURL TLS nil: plain text nil, or a config that verifies the server and allows TLS 1.2 or later CheckTLS Timeout 10s positive CheckTimeout AttemptTimeout 5s positive CheckAttemptTimeout MaxAttempts 3 1 or more CheckMaxAttempts BackoffBase 100ms positive CheckBackoffBase BackoffMax 5s positive, and at least BackoffBase, which NewClient checks CheckBackoffMax RetryBudget {MaxTokens: 10, TokenRatio: 0.1} MaxTokens from 3 to retry.TokenLimit, TokenRatio from 0.001 to retry.TokenLimit CheckRetryBudgetMaxTokens, CheckRetryBudgetTokenRatio Classify the table under How an attempt’s result counts set none: set in code Breaker {Window: 20, Probes: 1, OpenFor: 10s, ProbeTimeout: 10s} Window and Probes from 1 to circuit.MaxCount, the durations positive CheckBreakerWindow, CheckBreakerProbes, CheckBreakerOpenFor, CheckBreakerProbeTimeout BreakerPolicy see The circuit breaker Trip and Probe set none: set in code BaseURL has no default, so its chain has no .Default, and a variable that isn’t set fails as not found. CheckBaseURL rejects user info: a password in the URL would sit in a setting, and in every error that names the client’s origin. Credentials go in a header that service code sets.
Classify and BreakerPolicy are set in code, not sourced. What a dependency’s answers mean, and how it fails, are the end user’s knowledge, not an operator’s choice. NewClient runs every check again, and rejects a nil Classify, Trip or Probe, failing Init with exit 1, since the fault is in the code.
Two rules take two fields, and only NewClient checks them: a BackoffMax below BackoffBase, and a BaseURL whose scheme disagrees with TLS, as TLS and plain text describes. A check given to Validate sees one value, so neither fails in config.Struct. Both fail Init with exit 1, and an error that names the fields, such as Settings.TLS must be set for an https Settings.BaseURL, rather than with exit 78 naming a variable, even when an operator’s values caused them. An Init whose operators set both variables of either pair checks the pair itself after Read, and returns a *config.Error naming the variables. How a bad value fails explains the exit codes.
TLS and plain text Settings.TLS is the config the client dials the dependency with: the roots it trusts in RootCAs, and for mTLS, a client certificate in Certificates. The client dials with a clone of it, so the end user’s config is never changed. Init above reads the dependency’s CA from a file, through s.Host.FS, as Reading a file describes, and trusts only that CA:
// trusting returns a client's TLS config that trusts only the CA // certificates in pem. func trusting(pem []byte) (*tls.Config, error) { roots := x509.NewCertPool() if !roots.AppendCertsFromPEM(pem) { return nil, errors.New("holds no PEM certificate") } return &tls.Config{RootCAs: roots}, nil } readFile is the same helper as under Serving HTTP.
CheckTLS rejects a config that sets InsecureSkipVerify, or that allows nothing from TLS 1.2 on. A test trusts the CA it generates with humustest.NewCA through RootCAs, so nothing needs to skip verification.
A config with no RootCAs trusts the system’s roots, which crypto/x509 loads from the real host: the files SSL_CERT_FILE and SSL_CERT_DIR name in the real environment, and the OS’s certificate files. That is one of the ambient leaks. A service that calls only its own services sets RootCAs to its CA, as trusting does, and reads nothing ambient.
A nil TLS means plain text, with an http BaseURL. humus can’t control what a service connects to, and a mesh’s sidecar, a node-local agent or a cloud metadata endpoint is often plain HTTP. The URL names its scheme too, so NewClient requires the two to agree: an https BaseURL with a nil TLS, or an http one with a config, fails startup rather than quietly doing one of the two. Every humus server serves TLS, so a call to one is always https.
The client never reads HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY or NO_PROXY, and has no proxy setting. Its Jar is nil, so it keeps no cookies; the end user may set one.
Which requests are retried A call is retried only when sending it twice is both safe and possible:
Safe: its method is GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT or DELETE, which RFC 9110 defines as idempotent, or it carries an Idempotency-Key or X-Idempotency-Key header, which net/http treats the same way. Possible: it has no body, or its GetBody is set, which http.NewRequest does for a *bytes.Buffer, a *bytes.Reader and a *strings.Reader. The client rewinds the body with GetBody before each attempt after the first. Any other request makes one attempt, whatever Classify says of its result. Whether a request is safe to send twice is about the request, not about what the dependency answered, so a POST without an idempotency key can’t be charged twice. Its result still counts in the retry budget and in the breaker. net/http’s own list of requests it replays on a stale connection leaves out PUT and DELETE; RFC 9110 defines both as idempotent, and a service that sends them relies on that already.
Retries are bounded three ways:
MaxAttempts bounds the attempts of each request a call sends, 3 by default, and 1 turns retries off. A redirect is a request of its own, with attempts of its own. RetryBudget bounds every call to the dependency together, as retry.Budget describes: each attempt classified Retry takes a token, each Success adds a tenth of one back, and retries stop while half the tokens or fewer are left. So while the dependency fails, every call makes one attempt, rather than three, and the retries don’t multiply its load. Timeout bounds the call, as Timeouts describes. The wait before each retry is drawn from retry.Exponential’s schedule, with BackoffBase and BackoffMax: after attempt n, from 0 up to the smaller of BackoffMax and BackoffBase·2ⁿ⁻¹.
How an attempt’s result counts Every attempt’s result is classified twice: for retry, whether another attempt follows, and for the dependency’s circuit breaker, whether the result counts against the dependency. Settings.Classify returns both, in a Classification. Some of that is about the call, and the client decides it the same way for every dependency. The rest is about what the dependency’s answers mean, which differs from one API to another, and Classify decides it.
What the client decides Classify isn’t asked about:
an attempt the circuit breaker rejects, which ends the call; an error once the call’s context is done, because the caller gave up or the call’s deadline passed. Another attempt can’t help, so the call ends. The breaker ignores the caller giving up, and counts the deadline against the dependency; a body that fails once service code reads it, which the breaker counts as a failure, or ignores when the caller cancelled the call’s context. And whatever Classify returns:
a request that isn’t safe to send twice, or can’t be replayed, makes one attempt; a RetryAfter longer than BackoffMax ends the call, with the response as it came; a response whose body doesn’t fit in 64 KiB isn’t retried. The default DefaultSettings().Classify decides, of every response and every error while the call’s context is live:
An attempt’s result Retry Breaker a status below 500, other than 408 and 429 Success Success 408 Request Timeout Retry Success 429 Too Many Requests Retry, after Retry-After Success 500 Internal Server Error Stop Failure 502 Bad Gateway, 504 Gateway Timeout Retry Failure 503 Service Unavailable Retry, after Retry-After Failure any other 5xx, such as 501 Not Implemented Stop Success a server certificate the client doesn’t trust Stop Failure any other error, such as refused, reset or AttemptTimeout Retry Failure A 4xx is the dependency working: it answered, and the request was wrong, so another attempt won’t fix it, and the dependency counts as healthy. 408 and 429 are retried, and don’t count against it: a 408 says the server gave up waiting for the request, which RFC 9110 says a client may repeat, and a 429 is the server’s own flow control, which says when to come back. A 500 counts against the dependency but isn’t retried: it is usually the server’s bug, which a second attempt meets again. 502, 503 and 504 say the dependency, or what is in front of it, is unavailable, which is what retries are for. A certificate the client doesn’t trust is met again by every attempt. The default reads only the status and the headers, and never a body.
Writing a Classify An end user whose API means something else by an answer writes a Classify of their own, which usually handles what differs and hands the rest to the default. This ledger answers 409 while another write to the account is in flight, which is over by the next attempt:
d := httpclient.DefaultSettings() classify := d.Classify settings.Classify = func(resp *http.Response, err error) httpclient.Classification { if resp != nil && resp.StatusCode == http.StatusConflict { return httpclient.Classification{Retry: retry.Retry, Breaker: circuit.Success} } return classify(resp, err) } A 409 is then retried, as a GET or another request that is safe to send twice, and counts for the dependency rather than against it.
A Classify may read the body, for an API that answers 200 with an error in its body. It closes the body it read, and leaves in resp.Body what service code is to read, such as the bytes it read:
settings.Classify = func(resp *http.Response, err error) httpclient.Classification { if err != nil { return classify(resp, err) } b, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body) _ = resp.Body.Close() resp.Body = io.NopCloser(bytes.NewReader(b)) if readErr != nil { return httpclient.Classification{Retry: retry.Retry, Breaker: circuit.Failure} } if bytes.Contains(b, []byte(`"error"`)) { return httpclient.Classification{Retry: retry.Retry, Breaker: circuit.Success} } return classify(resp, err) } Its read counts against Timeout, but not against AttemptTimeout, which ends with the headers. The response body’s rules apply to the body it leaves, but not to its own read: io.ReadAll holds the whole body in memory, so a Classify for an API whose bodies can be large reads through an io.LimitReader. The client counts what this Classify returns, so a read that fails because the caller gave up counts as the Failure it returns here. A Classify for which that matters returns circuit.Ignored when resp.Request.Context().Err() is context.Canceled.
One Classify serves every API that shares a convention, such as a company’s own services. The function is the end user’s own, so it is written once and set on the client of each:
// The APIs behind the gateway share a convention: a 409 says another // write to the account is in flight, which is over by the next // attempt. One Classify says so, and is set on the client of each. classify := httpclient.DefaultSettings().Classify ourAPIs := func(resp *http.Response, err error) httpclient.Classification { if resp != nil && resp.StatusCode == http.StatusConflict { return httpclient.Classification{Retry: retry.Retry, Breaker: circuit.Success} } return classify(resp, err) } paymentsSettings.Classify = ourAPIs ledgerSettings.Classify = ourAPIs Classify is called on the goroutine that made the call, once for each attempt, so it must be safe for concurrent use. A Classification with a zero Outcome, or with retry.Retry and a negative RetryAfter, panics, as bedrock’s classifiers do. The client recovers nothing: the panic passes to the goroutine that made the call, once the attempt’s response is closed, so its connection isn’t held. humus ships no classifiers for well-known APIs, and no helpers to build one.
Retry-After, Timeout and AttemptTimeout Retry-After The default Classify reads the Retry-After header of the 429s and 503s it retries, and returns it as the Classification’s RetryAfter. Both of RFC 9110’s forms are read: a number of seconds, which is used as it is, and an HTTP-date, which is measured from now and clamped at 0. A malformed header is ignored. The wait before the next attempt is the longer of RetryAfter and the backoff. An end user’s Classify returns whatever its API says, such as a header of its own.
A RetryAfter longer than BackoffMax isn’t waited for, from any Classify: the call ends, and service code gets the response as it came. A server that asks for a minute is not one a call in flight should wait on. A wait that would end after the call’s deadline isn’t started either: the call returns the last response at once.
Timeout and AttemptTimeout Timeout bounds a whole call: every attempt, the waits between them, and reading the response’s body. It is the http.Client’s Timeout, which net/http puts on the request’s context as a deadline, unless the caller’s context has an earlier one, which then wins. So the retries see the deadline, and don’t start a wait that would end after it. It covers reading the body, so a client that streams large bodies raises it. CheckTimeout rejects a Timeout that is not positive: a client with no bound on a call holds a goroutine and a connection for as long as a dependency hangs.
AttemptTimeout bounds one attempt, from dialling until the response’s headers arrive. The attempt’s context is cancelled after it, with a cause that wraps context.DeadlineExceeded, and the attempt fails with an error that wraps it too. The call’s context is still live, so the error reaches Classify, and the default retries it, as any failed attempt. With the defaults, an attempt to a dependency that hangs fails after 5s, which leaves time for a second before Timeout’s 10s. The second has less than 5s left, so Timeout ends it, and the call, before AttemptTimeout would: against a dependency that hangs, the defaults make two attempts, not MaxAttempts' three. A client that wants every attempt sets Timeout above AttemptTimeout times MaxAttempts, plus the waits. AttemptTimeout stops counting once the headers arrive, so a slow body isn’t cut off: that is Timeout’s to bound.
The circuit breaker Each client has one circuit breaker, bedrock’s circuit.Breaker, which guards its dependency: while the dependency keeps failing, the client fails calls at once, rather than hold every caller for its timeouts and retries, and a probe now and then finds out when the dependency is back. The breaker sits inside the retries, so each attempt is a call it admits or rejects.
What counts is each attempt’s result, as the Breaker outcome of its Classification: Success, Failure, or Ignored for a result that says nothing about the dependency. The client decides some of it itself:
an error once the caller cancelled the call’s context is Ignored; an error once the call’s deadline passed, Timeout or one the caller set, is a Failure: a dependency that hangs ends every call this way, and a breaker that ignored deadlines would never open; a response’s result is counted with its body, with its Classification’s Breaker, once service code reads the body to the end or closes it. A read that fails is a Failure instead, whatever Classify said of the status, since the dependency sent its headers and then failed, or Ignored when the caller cancelled the call’s context. A body the client buffers before a retry is counted then. The default opens after 5 failures in a row, or once half of the last 20 or more results failed. It then rejects every attempt for OpenFor, 10s, and then lets one probe through at a time: a failed probe reopens it, and 3 successful ones close it. Settings.Breaker configures, from configuration, the Window of results the policy sees, how many Probes may be in flight at once, 1 by default, and the durations OpenFor and ProbeTimeout. Settings.BreakerPolicy decides when it opens and closes, in code: its Trip decides the 5 and the half of 20, and its Probe the 3 successful probes. A policy whose Trip always returns false turns the breaker off:
settings.BreakerPolicy.Trip = func(circuit.Counts) bool { return false } The policy runs with the breaker locked, on the goroutine of the call whose result it decides on, so it must be fast and safe for concurrent use. A panic in it passes to that goroutine, and circuit leaves the breaker consistent.
An attempt the breaker rejects sends nothing, and isn’t retried, which would defeat the breaker. Classify isn’t asked about it. The call returns at once, with an error that wraps a *circuit.RejectedError, through http.Client’s *url.Error. errors.Is(err, circuit.ErrRejected) tells service code nothing was sent, and the RejectedError’s RetryAfter says how much longer the breaker stays open.
A body that service code never closes leaves its result uncounted. That costs nothing while the breaker is closed. While it is half-open, the attempt was a probe, whose slot the body holds until it is read or closed, or for at most Breaker.ProbeTimeout, after which another probe may go. net/http asks for every body to be closed anyway.
Its log records The client logs through the Setup’s LoggerProvider, with the logger github.com/z5labs/humus/httpclient, one record for each change of the breaker’s state, in the context of the call that made it:
Record Severity When circuit breaker open WARN the breaker opens, from closed or from half-open circuit breaker half-open INFO OpenFor has passed, and the breaker lets a probe through circuit breaker closed INFO enough probes succeeded Each has the dependency’s server.address and server.port, the state the breaker left as circuit.previous_state, and the counts of that state: circuit.successes, circuit.failures, circuit.consecutive_successes, circuit.consecutive_failures and circuit.timed_out. The client logs nothing else: an error is returned to service code, not logged.
The response body Before another attempt follows, the client reads the body of the response it replaces into memory, up to 64 KiB, and closes it, before the wait. Closing it ends the attempt’s span, counts its result in the breaker, and frees its connection during the backoff. If the wait is cut short, such as by the caller’s context, the buffered response is what the call returns.
A body larger than 64 KiB isn’t retried: the call returns the response with its body intact. Error bodies are small, so 64 KiB keeps every one the client retries, and bounds what each call in flight holds.
A Classify that reads the body leaves what service code reads in resp.Body, and these rules apply to the body it leaves. Service code reads or closes every body, as net/http asks, which is also what counts the result in the breaker.
HTTP/2 behind a Kubernetes Service For an https BaseURL, the client offers HTTP/2 and then HTTP/1.1 in ALPN, so every server that offers h2 gets HTTP/2, a humus server set to HTTP2Only among them. An http BaseURL is HTTP/1.1 alone, since humus serves no unencrypted HTTP/2 (h2c).
HTTP/2 puts every call on one connection. A Kubernetes ClusterIP Service balances connections, not requests: kube-proxy picks a pod when a connection opens, and every request on it goes to that pod. So one client’s calls reach one pod of the dependency until that connection closes, and the calls spread across the dependency’s pods only as its callers’ connections do. Balancing each request across pods is out of humus’s scope: a mesh, or a proxy that balances requests, does it.
A humus server’s shutdown moves the calls during a rollout. When a pod of the dependency is stopped, an httpserver Service keeps serving through its drain, so the calls already on its connection are still answered while Kubernetes removes the pod from the Service’s endpoints. Its Shutdown then sends the client a GOAWAY, and waits for the calls in flight. The client opens its next connection through the Service, which reaches a pod still in its endpoints, and its calls move there. The same holds when the dependency scales up: a new pod gets a client’s calls only once the client’s connection closes, at a pod’s shutdown or once it has been idle for 90s.
Telemetry The client traces and measures every attempt with the Setup’s telemetry, through OpenTelemetry’s net/http instrumentation, otelhttp, given the TracerProvider, the MeterProvider and the Propagator of s.Telemetry. Nothing reaches OpenTelemetry’s globals: a process that sets them sees none of the client’s spans or metrics.
Each attempt is one span of kind CLIENT, every retry and redirect included, a child of the span in the request’s context, such as a handler’s request span or a job’s run span. A slow or failing dependency shows up in the caller’s trace. A request to another origin is refused before it is an attempt, so it has no span.
The span is named after the method, such as GET. The HTTP semantic conventions name a client span after its method and URL template, and a client has no template, only whatever URL service code built, which would make a span name per resource. It carries otelhttp’s attributes, among them url.full, with any user info removed, server.address, server.port, http.response.status_code and network.protocol.version, which is 2.0 for HTTP/2. Its status is Error for a 4xx or 5xx response, and for an attempt that fails with no response, such as a refused connection. An attempt that is not a call’s first carries http.request.resend_count, which otelhttp doesn’t set. A retry and a redirect each count, as the semantic conventions count them. An attempt the breaker rejects still has its span, which ends at once with status Error and error.type *circuit.RejectedError. The Setup’s propagator puts the attempt’s trace context and the request context’s baggage in each attempt’s headers, so a dependency served with httpserver joins the caller’s trace, with the attempt’s span as its server span’s parent, and its handler sees the caller’s baggage.
otelhttp records http.client.request.duration and http.client.request.body.size for each attempt, in its own scope, with the status code, or error.type for an attempt that failed with no response. A rejected attempt is among them, with an error.type that otelhttp writes differently from the span’s: the package path, github.com/z5labs/bedrock/circuit.RejectedError, where the span has *circuit.RejectedError. A query or an alert on rejections matches the form of the signal it reads. humus records no instrument of its own, for the breaker, the retry budget or anything else.
The breaker’s state changes are the client’s only log records, as Its log records lists.
Testing A service that calls a dependency is tested whole, inside testing/synctest, as Testing a humus App describes for any App. The client dials through the Setup’s Host, so the fake dependency is a second App on the same humustest Host: an httpserver Service whose handler answers as the dependency would, with a certificate from a CA that humustest.NewCA generates for the test. httpclient’s own tests start one with a helper:
// startPaymentsWith is startPayments, with the dependency's telemetry built // by tel. func startPaymentsWith(t *testing.T, h *humustest.Host, host humus.Host, tel telemetry.Builder, ca *humustest.CA, handler http.Handler) (stop func()) { t.Helper() cert := ca.Issue(t, "payments") p, status := humustest.Start(t, func(_ context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { settings := httpserver.DefaultSettings() settings.Addr = ":8443" settings.TLS = &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert.TLS()}} svc, err := httpserver.NewService(s, settings, handler) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{svc}, nil }, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(host), humus.WithTelemetry(tel))) <-h.Listening("payments:8443") return func() { p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) st := <-status require.Zero(t, st.Code(), "cause: %v", st.Cause()) } } It listens on :8443, every name on the Host’s network, so the client’s dial of payments:8443 reaches it, and its certificate is for payments, the host the client’s BaseURL names, so the client’s verification passes. startPayments is the same with no telemetry.
The end user’s whole App then runs against it, with the end user’s own Init above, and the environment production gives it. The test writes the App’s certificate and the dependency’s CA into the Host’s filesystem with humustest.WithFiles, and names them with humustest.WithEnv, as Giving the App its certificate describes. keyPairPEM and caPEM are helpers of the test file that PEM-encode them: keyPairPEM a certificate’s chain and private key, and caPEM the CA certificate that issued a certificate. orders and the dependency’s certificate are both issued by ca, so caPEM(orders) is the dependency’s CA too:
synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { ca := humustest.NewCA(t) orders := ca.Issue(t, "orders") h := humustest.NewHost(t, humustest.WithFiles(map[string][]byte{ "tls.pem": keyPairPEM(t, orders), "payments-ca.pem": caPEM(orders), })) stop := startPayments(t, h, h.Host(), ca, http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { _, _ = io.WriteString(w, "charge for "+r.URL.Path+": paid") })) defer stop() p, status := humustest.Start(t, Init, humustest.WithApp(httpserver.Defaults()), humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host()), humus.WithTelemetry(telemetry.NoopBuilder)), humustest.WithEnv(map[string]string{ "ADDR": ":9443", "TLS_PEM_FILE": "tls.pem", "PAYMENTS_URL": "https://payments:8443/v1", "PAYMENTS_CA_FILE": "payments-ca.pem", }), ) <-h.Listening("orders:9443") c := h.HTTPClient() c.Transport.(*http.Transport).TLSClientConfig = &tls.Config{RootCAs: ca.Pool()} resp, err := c.Get("https://orders:9443/orders/7/payment") require.NoError(t, err) b, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body) require.NoError(t, err) require.NoError(t, resp.Body.Close()) require.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode, "body: %s", b) require.Equal(t, "charge for /v1/charges/7: paid", string(b)) <-p.Notified(syscall.SIGTERM) p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) st := <-status require.Zero(t, st.Code(), "cause: %v", st.Cause()) }) The request reaches the App, the App’s handler calls the fake dependency through the client, and the answer comes back, all on the Host’s in-memory network, in no real time. The client trusts the CA through RootCAs, so the test reads no system root and skips no verification.
Fake time makes the client’s waits free too. A handler that answers 503 with Retry-After: 2 the first time costs the test 2s of fake time and no real time, and a dependency that hangs fails the attempt after AttemptTimeout just as instantly, so a test of retries, timeouts or the breaker opening runs as fast as one of a single call. A test that asserts on the client’s spans, metrics or breaker records gives the App humustest.NewTelemetry()’s Builder rather than telemetry.NoopBuilder.
description: How to call HTTP dependencies with the httpclient package: one client per dependency, built in Init from httpclient.Settings sourced with config.Struct, TLS and plain text, which requests are retried and how the end user's Classify decides what an answer means, Retry-After and the timeouts, the circuit breaker and its log records, the body rules, HTTP/2 behind a Kubernetes Service, what it records, and how to test the calls against a fake dependency.

body:
A service reports its health as monitors it combines into two probes, liveness and readiness, and an App’s readiness is owned by a health Service it returns from Init like any other Service. All of it is in the health package, which depends on nothing but the standard library and serves no protocol. httphealth and grpc/grpchealth expose the probes to Kubernetes.
The design behind this page is in Proposal: health monitors and probes, Revision 2, and, for exposing the probes, in Proposal: exposing health probes.
Monitors A Monitor is anything that can report whether it is healthy right now: a database ping, a flag the service sets once it has started, a check of a queue’s depth. It has one method, Healthy(ctx context.Context) (bool, error), which returns false, or an error, when the monitor is not healthy. Two monitors come with the package:
Binary is a monitor the service marks healthy or unhealthy itself, with MarkHealthy and MarkUnhealthy. Its zero value is unhealthy, and it is safe for concurrent use. MonitorFunc turns any func(context.Context) (bool, error) into a monitor. Its Healthy calls the function with the context it is given. A monitor honours the ctx it is given. Whatever checks a monitor, such as an orchestrator’s probe with a timeout, bounds the check with that context, so a monitor that dials or queries something passes ctx on rather than using a context of its own. A database ping that ignores it can hang a probe past its deadline.
Combining monitors Monitors combine, and the combinations are monitors themselves, so they nest:
And is healthy when every one of its monitors is. It checks them in order and stops at the first failure, the first monitor that is unhealthy or returns an error, and returns that monitor’s result without checking the rest. And with no monitors is healthy. Or is healthy when any one of its monitors is. It stops at the first that is healthy; otherwise it is unhealthy and joins the errors every monitor returned, with errors.Join. Or with no monitors is unhealthy. Both pass the context they are given to every monitor they check, nested ones included, so a caller’s deadline reaches each check.
Liveness and readiness An orchestrator such as Kubernetes asks a service two questions, and Probes holds a monitor for each:
Probe Question When it fails, Kubernetes Liveness is the process still working? restarts the container Readiness can the process serve traffic right now? stops sending it traffic until the probe passes again, without restarting it So a liveness probe should fail only when a restart would fix the process, a deadlock for example. Liveness checks no dependencies by default, which is And with no monitors: restarting a pod doesn’t fix a database that is down, and a liveness probe that checks one restarts every pod of the service while the database is down. Dependency checks go in readiness, which takes the pod out of the load balancer until the database is back.
Here readiness checks that the service has started and that its database answers ping, and liveness checks nothing:
var started health.Binary probes := health.Probes{ Liveness: health.And(), Readiness: health.And(&started, health.MonitorFunc(func(ctx context.Context) (bool, error) { return ping(ctx) == nil, nil })), } The health Service A health.Service is a Service that owns an App’s readiness. It is built for probes attached to a server the App already runs: a probes server owns readiness itself, so a pod with one returns no health Service. The end user’s Init builds one with NewService, adds monitors to its probes with Liveness and Readiness, and returns it next to the App’s other Services:
Init: func(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { hs := health.NewService( health.Liveness(&working), health.Readiness(health.MonitorFunc(func(ctx context.Context) (bool, error) { return ping(ctx) == nil, nil })), ) probes <- hs.Probes() // where an HTTP or gRPC Service would expose them return []humus.Service{hs}, nil }, Service.Probes returns its probes. Readiness is And of the Service’s own state and the monitors Readiness added, in the order they were added, so no monitor is checked while the Service itself is not ready. Liveness is And of the monitors Liveness added, and is healthy when there are none. The probes report the Service’s state when they are checked, so Probes may be called before the App runs. Liveness and Readiness panic on a nil monitor.
Readiness through the lifecycle The Service’s own readiness follows the lifecycle:
Not ready until it is serving. It is not ready from NewService until the App calls its Serve. Ready while it serves, as long as its readiness monitors are healthy. Not ready from the moment shutdown starts, through the drain. The App cancels Serve’s context as soon as it starts shutting down, before the drain, and the Service turns not ready then, for good. A load balancer checking readiness stops sending the App new traffic while the App’s HTTP and gRPC Services, which keep serving until Shutdown, answer what is still draining towards them. So the health Service is one of the Services that stop on the first shutdown signal: its Serve returns as soon as its context is done. A Service is served once; a Serve called after Shutdown, or after an earlier Serve, returns at once and leaves it not ready.
A health Service built but not returned from Init never turns ready. humus.App runs only the Services Init returns, so a Service it is never handed is never served, and its readiness probe fails for as long as the process lives. If an App’s readiness never passes, check that its health Service is in the slice Init returns.
Exposing the probes Two packages serve an App’s probes to an orchestrator, one per protocol:
httphealth, in the core module, answers Kubernetes’ httpGet probes; grpc/grpchealth, in the grpc module, answers gRPC health v1, which Kubernetes’ grpc probes, grpc-health-probe and grpc-go’s client-side health checking all ask. Each has two shapes: a handler or server attached to a server the App already runs, answering from a health Service’s Probes, and a probes server on a port of its own, which owns readiness itself. The design behind this section is in Proposal: exposing health probes, with its revision 1 and revision 2.
Probes are explicit. The end user’s Init returns a health Service next to the server its probes are attached to, or a probes server, like any other Service. No runtime package’s Main exposes probes by default: humus imposes no port, so it has nowhere to serve them.
Which wiring fits the pod Attach the probes to a server the pod already runs, rather than opening another port. A probes port is only for:
a pod with no server, such as a consumer’s or a long-running job’s; a server that requires client certificates, which the kubelet never presents; a gRPC service on a cluster whose grpc probes can’t use TLS. The pod Its main The probes Kubernetes a consumer, or a long-running job humus.Main httphealth.NewService on a port of its own httpGet, scheme: HTTPS, on that port an HTTPS API httpserver.Main a health Service, and httphealth.NewHandler attached to the API’s mux; httphealth.NewService instead when the API requires client certificates httpGet, scheme: HTTPS, on the API’s port or the probes port a gRPC service, on a cluster whose grpc probes can use TLS grpcserver.Main a health Service, and grpchealth.NewServer registered on the end user’s Service; grpchealth.NewService instead when the Service requires client certificates grpc with service: liveness or readiness, over TLS on the Service’s port, or on the probes port a gRPC service, on any other cluster grpcserver.Main grpchealth.NewService on a plaintext port of its own grpc with service: liveness or readiness, on that port a Kubernetes Job’s pod, usually humus.Main none none A probes server adds no drain, since nothing routes traffic to it, so a consumer’s or a job’s pod with a probes server stays on humus.Main.
Attached probes httphealth.NewHandler answers the probes from a health Service’s Probes. It routes on the full path, so it is mounted at "/health/" of the mux the API is served on, without http.StripPrefix, next to the API, and the health Service is returned from Init next to the API’s Service:
db := openStore() // the end user's database hs := health.NewService(health.Readiness(health.MonitorFunc(func(ctx context.Context) (bool, error) { if err := db.Ping(ctx); err != nil { return false, err // logged, never in the probe's answer } return true, nil }))) api := http.NewServeMux() api.HandleFunc("GET /hello", hello) mux := http.NewServeMux() mux.Handle("/", api) mux.Handle("/health/", httphealth.NewHandler(s, hs.Probes())) svc, err := httpserver.NewService(s, settings, mux) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{svc, hs}, nil The pod then needs no second port: the kubelet probes the API’s own port, with scheme: HTTPS, and doesn’t verify its certificate. The handler recovers no panic of a monitor: the server it is attached to does.
grpchealth.NewServer is the gRPC health v1 server. It is registered on the end user’s grpcserver.Service, next to their own services, and answers from a health Service returned next to it:
svc, err := grpcserver.NewService(s, settings) if err != nil { return nil, err } testpb.RegisterTestServiceServer(svc, greeter{}) // the end user's own service hs := health.NewService() healthpb.RegisterHealthServer(svc, grpchealth.NewServer(s, hs.Probes())) return []humus.Service{svc, hs}, nil A grpcserver.Service serves only TLS, and the kubelet’s grpc probes connect in plain text unless the cluster has the GRPCContainerProbeTLS feature gate on. So the kubelet reaches an attached server only on a cluster with that gate on, and only when the Service requires no client certificate. grpc-go’s clients reach it on every cluster, for client-side health checking.
One health Service’s Probes can go to NewHandler and NewServer both, to answer HTTP and gRPC probes from one state.
Probes servers httphealth.NewService and grpchealth.NewService serve the probes, and nothing else, on a port of their own. A probes server owns the App’s readiness, as a health Service does. It builds a health Service from the health.Options it is given, health.Liveness and health.Readiness, and runs it for as long as it serves, so the end user’s Init returns no health Service next to it. Here a worker, a stand-in for a consumer, is ready once it has connected:
w := newWorker() probes, err := httphealth.NewService(s, probeSettings, health.Readiness(w.Connected())) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{w, probes}, nil A probes server’s readiness follows the lifecycle as a health Service’s does: false until its Serve starts, false for good once Serve’s context is done, which is when the App starts shutting down, or once Shutdown is called, and otherwise And of the monitors health.Readiness added, in order. Liveness checks the monitors health.Liveness added, and is healthy when there are none. A pod that serves its probes in two ways, such as an HTTP probes port and NewServer registered on its gRPC Service for client-side health checking, gives each the same monitors.
A probes server serves through the drain. It keeps serving until Shutdown, like an HTTP or gRPC Service, so once the App starts shutting down a readiness probe is answered not ready, rather than refused, and a liveness probe is still answered healthy.
Settings and their checks httphealth.Settings has two fields, Addr and TLS, and grpchealth.Settings one, Addr. None has a default, so neither package has a DefaultSettings, and the end user sources every field, with no .Default in their chains, as Configuring a humus service describes. Each field has a check that reports what is wrong with a value without naming the field: CheckAddr in both packages, and httphealth.CheckTLS. An unset variable then fails as not found, with exit 78:
probeSettings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) httphealth.Settings { return httphealth.Settings{ // No .Default: both fields are required. Addr: r.Get(env("PROBES_ADDR").Validate(httphealth.CheckAddr)), TLS: r.Get(env("PROBES_TLS_PEM_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Parse(serverTLS).Validate(httphealth.CheckTLS)), } }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78, naming every bad variable } readFile and serverTLS are the end user’s helpers, as on Serving HTTP. CheckAddr rejects an address that isn’t host:port, "" included, and a port that isn’t a number from 0 to 65535. NewService runs every check again, rejects a nil Option, and listens on Addr through the Setup’s Host, in Init.
TLS on the HTTP probes port The HTTP probes server serves HTTPS, as every HTTP port humus serves does, so its probes set scheme: HTTPS. The kubelet doesn’t verify the certificate of such a probe, so the end user’s own certificate serves, the one their other ports serve or any other: the probes need none of their own. A tls.Config shared with an API that requires client certificates can’t be passed as it is, though, as the next paragraph explains: pass a Clone of it with ClientAuth set to tls.NoClientCert. The server serves a clone of Settings.TLS, offering only http/1.1 in ALPN, since the kubelet speaks HTTP/1.1, and it serves no HTTP/2. A probe that leaves out scheme: HTTPS is answered 400 by net/http, so it fails, and the failed TLS handshake is logged at ERROR, so the log says why.
CheckTLS rejects a config that requires a client certificate, one whose ClientAuth is RequireAnyClientCert or RequireAndVerifyClientCert. The kubelet presents none, so every probe would fail and the pod would never turn ready. VerifyClientCertIfGiven, and every weaker ClientAuth, is accepted. CheckTLS also rejects a nil config and one with no certificate, where none of Certificates, GetCertificate and GetConfigForClient is set.
The gRPC probes port, in plain text The gRPC probes server serves plain text, because the kubelet’s grpc probes use TLS only with the GRPCContainerProbeTLS feature gate, which is alpha and off by default. It answers gRPC health v1 and nothing else: no service of the end user’s is registered on it, so nothing of theirs is reachable in plain text, and their own services stay TLS-only on the grpcserver.Service’s port:
svc, err := grpcserver.NewService(s, cfg.grpc) if err != nil { return nil, err } testpb.RegisterTestServiceServer(svc, greeter{}) // the end user's own service probes, err := grpchealth.NewService(s, cfg.probes) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{svc, probes}, nil cfg.probes is the probes server’s Settings, sourced next to the grpcserver.Settings:
probes: grpchealth.Settings{ // No .Default: the field is required. Addr: r.Get(env("PROBES_ADDR").Validate(grpchealth.CheckAddr)), }, The port stays plaintext until Kubernetes’ grpc probes use TLS without a feature gate. TLS is made required on it then, by a proposal of its own. Shutdown ends every stream, a Watch included, with Unavailable, as a grpcserver.Service does, and then stops the server gracefully.
The HTTP answers Request Healthy Unhealthy, or the monitor returned an error GET or HEAD /health/liveness 200, OK 503, Service Unavailable GET or HEAD /health/readiness 200, OK 503, Service Unavailable another method on either path 405 405 any other path, /health/ itself included 404 404 The body is the status text and a newline, OK\n or Service Unavailable\n, with Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 and Cache-Control: no-store. The kubelet decides on the status code alone, so the body says no more than which code it is, for a person with curl. A HEAD gets the same status and headers, and no body. A 405 carries an Allow header. A monitor’s error is never in the body. It can name a host or a credential’s user, and a probe port is reachable by anything that can reach the pod. The error is in the log, as Telemetry describes. The paths are humus’s from before the reset. No path is a standard for workloads: /livez and /readyz are what Kubernetes’ own components serve. The gRPC answers Request Check Watch service "" readiness readiness service readiness readiness readiness service liveness liveness liveness any other service NotFound one SERVICE_UNKNOWN, and the stream stays open the monitor is healthy SERVING SERVING it is unhealthy, or returns an error NOT_SERVING; an error is logged NOT_SERVING; an error is logged when the status changes "" is readiness. It is the overall status, which a grpc probe without service, grpc-health-probe and grpc-go’s client-side health checking all ask for. liveness and readiness are the names Kubernetes suggests for answering both probes on one port. Any other name is NotFound, the name of a service registered on the same server, such as cart.v1.CartService, included: health has no status per gRPC service. Watch polls once a second. Monitors are checked when asked and send no changes, so a Watch sends the current status at once, and then each change of it. Every Watch of one name on one server shares one poller, which runs while the name has watchers, so a hundred clients watching "" cost one check a second, not a hundred. Each poll checks with a context that is done after a second, and a check that runs out of time is NOT_SERVING. With a one-second poll, a client using client-side health checking learns that a pod is draining within a second of shutdown starting, well within grpcserver.Main’s 5s drain. List answers the three names, each with its current status. Manifests An HTTPS API with the handler attached is probed on its own port:
livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /health/liveness port: 8443 # the API's port scheme: HTTPS readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /health/readiness port: 8443 scheme: HTTPS A pod with an HTTP probes server is probed on that port, here named probes in the container’s ports:
ports: - name: probes containerPort: 8081 livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /health/liveness port: probes scheme: HTTPS readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /health/readiness port: probes scheme: HTTPS A gRPC service with a plaintext probes port names the probe in its service field:
livenessProbe: grpc: port: 8081 # the probes port; the end user's services are served over TLS on their own service: liveness readinessProbe: grpc: port: 8081 service: readiness On a cluster with GRPCContainerProbeTLS on, the same grpc probes go to the grpcserver.Service’s own port instead, where grpchealth.NewServer is registered, with the TLS setting the gate adds; see Kubernetes' Use TLS with gRPC probes and gRPC services.
Startup probes There is no startup probe of its own, and Probes has no field for one. A probes server answers only once its Serve runs, and the App calls Serve only after Init has returned. While Init runs, a probe’s connection waits in the listener’s backlog, or is refused if the listener isn’t open yet, and the probe times out or fails. So a startup probe on the liveness path succeeds exactly when Init is done, which is Kubernetes' own advice:
startupProbe: httpGet: path: /health/liveness port: probes scheme: HTTPS failureThreshold: 30 # 30 × 2s: Init has a minute periodSeconds: 2 A service whose Init is slow, such as one that waits for a database or runs migrations, sets a startup probe, so liveness doesn’t restart it before it has started. One that starts fast needs none.
Checks No timeout of the handler’s own, and no caching. Each probe request checks its monitor once, with the request’s context. The kubelet’s timeoutSeconds closes the connection, which cancels an HTTP request’s context, and sets a gRPC call’s deadline, so a monitor that honours its context is bounded by the probe. The kubelet checks each probe every periodSeconds, 10s by default, so a database ping in readiness costs one ping per pod every 10 seconds. A monitor that is too expensive to check that often caches its own result, in the end user’s MonitorFunc. A cache in humus would need a setting for its age, and would answer a probe with a result older than the probe asked for. The one shared check is Watch’s poller, above. A probes port isn’t for the public. A probes server answers anyone who can reach the port, and every request checks a monitor. The port is the container’s, for the kubelet, and isn’t routed by a Kubernetes Service or an ingress. Telemetry A monitor’s error is one ERROR record, through the Setup’s LoggerProvider, under the package’s import path, github.com/z5labs/humus/httphealth or github.com/z5labs/humus/grpc/grpchealth, in the request’s context. Its body is the error, and its attribute health.probe is liveness or readiness. A monitor that is unhealthy without an error, such as the health Service’s own readiness once the App starts shutting down, logs nothing. Probes servers record no spans and no metrics, and extract no trace context: a probe every few seconds would be most of a quiet service’s traces. They log listening at INFO when they start, and the HTTP probes server logs each line of net/http’s error log, such as a TLS handshake error, at ERROR. Attached probes are traced like any request. The handler mounted on an httpserver.Service, or the server registered on a grpcserver.Service, sits inside that Service’s instrumentation, which records every request, and a monitor’s ERROR record carries the trace of the probe’s span. A team that doesn’t want the probes’ spans drops them in its sampler. A consumer’s readiness A Kafka consumer is ready once it has joined its group. Joined returns a health.Monitor that is unhealthy until franz-go first hands the member an assignment, empty or not, and healthy from then until Serve returns. A consumer’s pod has no server of its own, so its probes go on a probes server, with health.Readiness(consumer.Joined()):
consumer, err := kafka.NewService(s, settings, nop) if err != nil { return nil, err } probes, err := httphealth.NewService(s, probeSettings, health.Readiness(consumer.Joined())) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{consumer, probes}, nil Nothing routes traffic to a consumer, so its readiness gates rollouts and disruption budgets. A rollout whose new pods can’t reach the brokers then stalls at its progress deadline, with the old pods still consuming, rather than replacing them with pods that never consume. A broker outage after the first join doesn’t make the consumer unready: it hits every pod at once, and would only block a rollout that might be the fix.
Joined is for readiness only. In liveness, it would restart a pod that starts while the brokers are unreachable, before it has ever joined, and the kubelet’s restart backoff would then hold it down after the brokers come back. A liveness monitor that turned unhealthy whenever the member is out of its group would do the same to every pod in a broker outage, while franz-go rejoins on its own. The errors a restart would fix already end Serve, so the pod exits and is restarted without a probe.
Jobs A Kubernetes Job’s pod usually needs no probes. Nothing routes to it, and a job that hangs is ended by its activeDeadlineSeconds, when it sets one. So a job’s Init returns the job and nothing else, and needs no health Service: nothing in the lifecycle asks for readiness.
A long-running job that wants a liveness probe returns httphealth.NewService’s Service next to its job.Service, and stays on humus.Main. The probe is only as good as its liveness monitor: with none, it checks only that the process answers, so a job that can hang gives it a monitor of its own progress, here progress, which the run keeps healthy while it makes progress:
probes, err := httphealth.NewService(s, probeSettings, health.Liveness(progress)) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{ probes, job.NewService(s, run), }, nil When the job finishes, the App ends, and the probes server with it.
Testing the probes A probes server is tested in a whole App, run with humustest.Start on a humustest Host, under testing/synctest, with a certificate from humustest.NewCA. This is httphealth’s own test that an API’s pod with a probes port is not ready during the drain:
func TestInit_is_not_ready_during_the_drain(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { ca := humustest.NewCA(t) h := humustest.NewHost(t) // apiInit returns an API on :8443 and a probes server on :8081, and // no health Service: the probes server owns readiness. apiInit := func(_ context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { settings := httpserver.DefaultSettings() settings.Addr = ":8443" settings.TLS = &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{ca.Issue(t, "localhost").TLS()}} api, err := httpserver.NewService(s, settings, http.NotFoundHandler()) if err != nil { return nil, err } probes, err := httphealth.NewService(s, probeSettings(t, ca)) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{api, probes}, nil } p, status := humustest.Start(t, apiInit, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host()), humus.WithTelemetry(telemetry.NoopBuilder), httpserver.Defaults()), ) <-h.Listening("localhost:8081") synctest.Wait() c := kubelet(h, ca) require.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, probe(t, c, readinessURL)) p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) time.Sleep(time.Second) // inside the 5s drain require.Equal(t, http.StatusServiceUnavailable, probe(t, c, readinessURL)) require.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, probe(t, c, livenessURL)) st := <-status require.Zero(t, st.Code(), "cause: %v", st.Cause()) require.Empty(t, p.Stderr()) }) } The API stands in for one that requires client certificates, the case for a probes port next to an API; one that doesn’t attaches its probes, and is tested the same way, with the probes requested on the API’s port. probeSettings returns httphealth.Settings on :8081 with a certificate for localhost from the CA, and probe makes the request, reads and closes the body, and returns the status code. kubelet is the Host’s HTTP client, given the CA’s pool as its roots, speaking HTTP/1.1 alone, as the kubelet does:
// kubelet returns h's HTTP client, trusting only ca, and speaking HTTP/1.1 // alone, as the kubelet does. func kubelet(h *humustest.Host, ca *humustest.CA) *http.Client { c := h.HTTPClient() tr := c.Transport.(*http.Transport) tr.TLSClientConfig = &tls.Config{RootCAs: ca.Pool(), NextProtos: []string{"http/1.1"}} var protos http.Protocols protos.SetHTTP1(true) tr.Protocols = &protos return c } A gRPC probes port is asked with grpcservertest.NewClient, given insecure.NewCredentials() and nil roots, since the port serves plain text, as the kubelet’s probes speak it:
// plaintext returns a client of the health server on address in h that // speaks plain text, as the kubelet's grpc probes do. func plaintext(t *testing.T, h *humustest.Host, address string) healthpb.HealthClient { t.Helper() return healthpb.NewHealthClient(grpcservertest.NewClient(t, h, address, nil, grpc.WithTransportCredentials(insecure.NewCredentials()), )) } An attached server is asked the same way, with the CA’s pool in place of nil and no transport credentials, over TLS on the Service’s port.
Both probes servers pass the Service contract, checked with humustest.TestService. They keep serving after Serve’s context is done, so its subtest for Shutdown after Serve has returned on its own reports SKIP:
func TestService(t *testing.T) { humustest.TestService(t, func(t *testing.T, s *humus.Setup) humus.Service { cert := humustest.NewCA(t).Issue(t, "localhost") svc, err := httphealth.NewService(s, httphealth.Settings{ Addr: ":8081", TLS: &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert.TLS()}}, }) require.NoError(t, err) return svc }) } Migration from rest.Liveness, rest.Readiness and internal/grpchealth Before the reset Now GET /health/liveness and /health/readiness on every rest.Api, 200 by default httphealth.NewHandler attached to the API’s mux, or httphealth.NewService on a port of its own, answering from a health Service rest.Liveness(h), rest.Readiness(h) with a handler of the end user’s health.Liveness(m), health.Readiness(m) with a Monitor, given to the probes server, or to the health Service when the probes are attached grpc.Api.RegisterService health-checking an implementation that is a health.Monitor nothing implicit: the monitor goes in the health Service’s readiness internal/grpchealth grpchealth.NewServer, or grpchealth.NewService on a plaintext port no answer for the service "" "" is readiness, and liveness and readiness are named a monitor’s error as SERVICE_UNKNOWN NOT_SERVING, and the error logged Watch polling every 10s, per stream every second, once per server and name the global humus.Logger s.Telemetry.LoggerProvider Testing A health Service is tested in a whole App, with bedrocktest’s fake process and a humustest Host, under testing/synctest, so the drain passes in fake time and readiness can be checked while it runs. This is health’s own test that the Service is not ready during the drain:
func TestServiceIsNotReadyDuringTheDrainDelay(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { hs := health.NewService() readiness := hs.Probes().Readiness api := newServer() // keeps serving, so the drain lasts its whole delay app := humus.App{ Host: humustest.NewHost(t).Host(), Telemetry: telemetry.NoopBuilder, ShutdownGracePeriod: 10 * time.Second, Drain: humus.DrainDelay(5 * time.Second), Init: func(context.Context, *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { return []humus.Service{api, hs}, nil }, } p := bedrocktest.NewProcess(t) status := make(chan bedrock.ExitStatus, 1) go func() { status <- app.Run(t.Context(), p.Process()) }() <-p.Notified(syscall.SIGTERM) synctest.Wait() // Serve has started ready, err := readiness.Healthy(t.Context()) require.NoError(t, err) require.True(t, ready) sigterm := time.Now() p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) synctest.Wait() // shutdown has started; the drain is running ready, err = readiness.Healthy(t.Context()) require.NoError(t, err) require.False(t, ready) require.Zero(t, (<-status).Code()) require.Equal(t, 5*time.Second, time.Since(sigterm)) }) } <-p.Notified(syscall.SIGTERM) waits until the App listens for signals, and synctest.Wait until every goroutine in the test, Serve included, is blocked, so the first check sees the Service serving. After the SIGTERM, synctest.Wait returns while the App waits out its five-second drain, and readiness is already false. The drain ends once every Serve has returned, and the health Service’s Serve returns as soon as shutdown starts, so the test runs it next to api, a Service that keeps serving until Shutdown as an HTTP or gRPC Service does: that is what keeps the drain running for its whole five seconds. A test of an App’s own readiness monitors works the same way: take the probes from the Service, run the App, and check them at each point of the lifecycle.
