body:
The grpcserver package serves gRPC over TLS as a humus.Service. The end user’s Init sources its Settings, builds the Service with grpcserver.NewService, registers their generated services on it, as they would on a *grpc.Server, and returns it. grpcserver.Main runs it with the defaults a gRPC server behind a Kubernetes Service needs: a 5s drain and a 15s grace period. Its test package, grpcservertest, runs the same App in a test, on the same defaults, with a client that dials the test Host over TLS.
Both packages are in the nested module github.com/z5labs/humus/grpc, so a service that doesn’t serve gRPC doesn’t get grpc-go or otelgrpc in its module graph. The module exports no App, and grpcserver runs no health Service and serves no probes: the module’s grpchealth does, as Health probes describes. The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: gRPC services, with its revision.
A service The end user’s Init sources grpcserver.Settings with config.Struct, as Configuring a humus service describes, builds the Service with NewService, registers their services on it, and returns it:
// Init is the end user's Init: it sources the Settings, builds the Service // with NewService, registers the end user's service on it and returns it, // with any other Service the process runs. func Init(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) } settings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) grpcserver.Settings { return grpcserver.Settings{ // No .Default: both fields are required, so an unset variable fails as not found. Addr: r.Get(env("GRPC_ADDR").Validate(grpcserver.CheckAddr)), // readFile and serverTLS are the end user's own helpers. The // bundle's password is read only once the bundle has been. TLS: r.Get(env("GRPC_TLS_P12_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).FlatMap(func(bundle []byte) config.Value[*tls.Config] { return env("GRPC_TLS_P12_PASSWORD").Parse(serverTLS(bundle)) }).Validate(grpcserver.CheckTLS)), } }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78, naming every bad variable } svc, err := grpcserver.NewService(s, settings) if err != nil { return nil, err } testpb.RegisterTestServiceServer(svc, greeter{}) return []humus.Service{svc}, nil } testpb is grpc-go’s interop/grpc_testing service, standing in for the end user’s generated code: a RegisterCartServiceServer(svc, carts) call is written the same way. The variable names are the service’s own: humus defines none of them. readFile and serverTLS are the end user’s helpers too, shown under TLS.
The service’s main is one call to grpcserver.Main, here with a telemetry Builder that names the service, as Telemetry describes:
grpcserver.Main(Init, humus.WithTelemetry(buildTelemetry)) NewService runs every check on the Settings again, and then listens on Settings.Addr through the Setup’s Host, in Init. So a port that is already taken fails Init, and the App exits 1, and a connection that arrives before Serve runs waits in the backlog rather than being refused. The listener’s close is registered with s.OnStop, so an Init that fails after NewService still closes it. An Addr with port 0 listens on a free port, which Service.Addr reports.
Init returns the gRPC Service along with any other Service the process runs, such as a Kafka consumer next to the gRPC server, or the health Service. Any Service returning ends the App.
Settings grpcserver.Settings follows the settings convention: plain Go values, and a check for each field. The package reads no environment variable and no file, and defines no variable name.
Field Default Valid Check Addr none: required host:port, with any host, an empty one included, and a port written as a number from 0 to 65535 CheckAddr TLS none: required a config that has a certificate and allows TLS 1.2 or later CheckTLS CheckAddr accepts what Host.Listen accepts: an empty host listens on every name, and port 0 picks a free port. It rejects "", an address with no port, and a port that isn’t such a number, such as the named port :grpc.
Everything else about the server, such as its interceptors, keepalive parameters and message size limits, is code, and goes in opts, as Server options describes. An end user who wants a variable for one of them sources it in their Init and passes the option.
Addr and TLS are both required. Neither has a default: humus imposes no port, and serves nothing in plain text. So the package has no DefaultSettings(), which would only return the zero Settings, whose Addr of "" and nil TLS both checks reject. The end user’s chains for them have no .Default, as in Init above, so a variable that isn’t set fails as not found. The App exits 78, and config.Struct names every variable at fault in one error. With neither set:
init: config GRPC_ADDR: not found config GRPC_TLS_P12_FILE: not found NewService runs the same checks itself, so a Settings built in code with a bad field fails Init too, naming the field, such as grpcserver: NewService: Settings.Addr "nope" is not host:port. That error is no *config.Error, so the App exits 1: the fault is in the code, not in the configuration. How a bad value fails explains the exit codes.
TLS TLS is required. The Service serves gRPC with Settings.TLS and nothing in plain text. There is no plaintext setting and no self-signed fallback: a service that hasn’t sourced a certificate doesn’t start, rather than starting and failing every RPC. Traffic is encrypted all the way to the pod, whatever sits in front of it, so every service needs a certificate, even behind a mesh that already encrypts between pods.
The certificate The end user decodes the certificate from a file, read through s.Host.FS so that a test reads it from its own directory and production from the real disk, as Reading a file describes. How the certificate is stored and encoded is the end user’s decision. Init above reads a PKCS#12 bundle from the file GRPC_TLS_P12_FILE names, and decodes it with the password in GRPC_TLS_P12_PASSWORD, so a missing file, a missing password and a wrong one each fail as a config error with exit 78:
// readFile returns a parser for config.Value.Parse that reads the whole // file a variable names, through fsys. func readFile(fsys humus.FS) func(name string) ([]byte, error) { return func(name string) ([]byte, error) { f, err := fsys.Open(name) if err != nil { return nil, err } defer func() { _ = f.Close() }() return io.ReadAll(f) } } // serverTLS returns a parser for config.Value.Parse that decodes bundle, a // PKCS#12 bundle, with the password it is given, into a server's TLS // config. func serverTLS(bundle []byte) func(password string) (*tls.Config, error) { return func(password string) (*tls.Config, error) { key, leaf, chain, err := pkcs12.DecodeChain(bundle, password) if err != nil { return nil, err } cert := tls.Certificate{Certificate: [][]byte{leaf.Raw}, PrivateKey: key, Leaf: leaf} for _, c := range chain { cert.Certificate = append(cert.Certificate, c.Raw) } return &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert}}, nil } } pkcs12.DecodeChain is from go-pkcs12, which humus doesn’t depend on. A PEM file that holds the certificate chain and the private key needs no password: its chain is env("GRPC_TLS_PEM_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Parse(serverTLS).Validate(grpcserver.CheckTLS), with a serverTLS that calls tls.X509KeyPair, as Serving HTTP shows. A certificate that rotates on disk is served from a config that sets GetCertificate instead of Certificates.
What CheckTLS rejects CheckTLS fails startup on a config that would otherwise fail every connection. It rejects:
nil, which is what the zero Settings leaves TLS; a config with no certificate: none of Certificates, GetCertificate and GetConfigForClient set, with which every handshake fails; a MaxVersion below TLS 1.2, which HTTP/2, and so gRPC, requires. grpc-go’s clients ask for at least TLS 1.2 by default. Its CipherSuites are not checked. Like every check, its error doesn’t name the field: the chain that sourced the config names its variable.
Client certificates A Service that requires its clients to present a certificate sets ClientAuth, as with any tls.Config: tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert, with the CAs it trusts in ClientCAs. CheckTLS accepts such a config. Kubernetes' probes present no client certificate, as Health probes describes.
grpc.Creds has no effect Settings.TLS is the one way to set how the Service secures its connections. NewService passes its transport credentials, built from Settings.TLS, after the end user’s options, and grpc-go keeps the last grpc.Creds it is given. So a grpc.Creds in opts, such as grpc.Creds(insecure.NewCredentials()), has no effect: the Service still serves TLS, and a plaintext client fails to connect with Unavailable. The end user’s config is cloned, so it is never changed.
Server options Everything about the server that isn’t a setting is a grpc.ServerOption the end user passes to NewService, after the Settings: their interceptors, with grpc.ChainUnaryInterceptor and grpc.ChainStreamInterceptor, keepalive parameters, with grpc.KeepaliveParams and grpc.KeepaliveEnforcementPolicy, message size limits, with grpc.MaxRecvMsgSize and grpc.MaxSendMsgSize, and a second stats handler, as in grpcserver.NewService(s, settings, grpc.ChainUnaryInterceptor(authenticate)).
NewService builds the server with humus’s options first, then opts, then humus’s transport credentials:
Option Why grpc.StatsHandler, with otelgrpc’s server handler traces and metrics, from s.Telemetry: see Telemetry grpc.ChainUnaryInterceptor and grpc.ChainStreamInterceptor, with panic recovery, and for streams the context that Shutdown cancels see Panics and Streams at shutdown grpc.WaitForHandlers(true) Stop waits for every handler to return, so no handler outlives Shutdown the end user’s opts grpc.Creds, from Settings.TLS last, so an end user’s grpc.Creds can’t replace it grpc-go keeps one value of some options and chains others, so where an option in opts lands depends on which it is:
An option that chains, such as grpc.ChainUnaryInterceptor, grpc.ChainStreamInterceptor or grpc.StatsHandler, adds to humus’s. The end user’s interceptors run inside humus’s, after panic recovery, and a stats handler in opts is called after humus’s. An option that grpc-go keeps one value of, such as grpc.MaxRecvMsgSize or grpc.KeepaliveParams, takes the last value it is given, so one in opts wins over the same option in humus’s. Of those, humus sets only grpc.WaitForHandlers, before opts, and grpc.Creds, after them. grpc.WaitForHandlers(false) breaks the Service contract. It replaces humus’s grpc.WaitForHandlers(true), and lets a handler outlive Shutdown, the App’s grace period and the process’s telemetry. humustest.TestService reports the handler’s goroutine as a leak. Registration The *Service is a grpc.ServiceRegistrar, so generated code registers services on it, as Init above does. RegisterService must be called before Serve, as with a *grpc.Server.
RegisterService panics instead of exiting. grpc-go calls os.Exit on three registration mistakes, which would bypass the lifecycle, the OnStop functions and telemetry: a registration after Serve, a service registered twice, and an implementation that doesn’t implement the service’s interface. The Service checks for the same three first, and panics instead, with the service’s name in the message. All three are programming errors, so the panic fails the end user’s Init in the first test or the first start.
Server reflection is off by default. Reflection exposes the service’s schema to anyone who can reach its port, so the Service registers none. An end user who wants it registers it in their Init, after their own services, which Service.GetServiceInfo makes work:
reflection.Register(svc) reflection is google.golang.org/grpc/reflection.
Shutdown The Service follows the two shutdown signals of a humus App:
Serve’s context being done changes nothing. It is done as soon as the App starts shutting down, and the Service keeps serving connections and RPCs through the App’s drain, while load balancers stop sending it traffic. An RPC that arrives during the drain is served, and an RPC in flight finishes. Shutdown ends every stream, as Streams at shutdown describes, and then calls GracefulStop. That stops accepting connections, sends every client a GOAWAY, and waits for the RPCs in flight to finish. gRPC connections are long-lived, and the GOAWAY is what moves a client off a terminating pod: it opens its next connection elsewhere. When the grace period runs out first, Shutdown calls Stop, which closes every connection and cancels every RPC’s context. With grpc.WaitForHandlers(true), which humus sets, Stop then waits for every handler to return. The App exits 1 with a *humus.GracePeriodError. A handler returns once its context is done. Stop waits for every handler, so a handler that ignores its context holds the App up past the grace period, and in a test that runs the App inside testing/synctest, synctest reports its goroutine as a leak.
Streams at shutdown A stream that runs until its client leaves, such as a subscription, would hold GracefulStop up until the grace period, and every deployment would exit 1. So Shutdown ends every stream, with a status the client can act on. A stream interceptor of humus’s gives every streaming RPC’s handler a context of its own, derived from the RPC’s, which Shutdown cancels. That covers server, client and bidirectional streams. When Shutdown starts:
it cancels the context of every stream in flight, before it calls GracefulStop. A stream that starts after that gets a context that is already cancelled; when a handler then returns nil, an error that is context.Canceled, or a status with codes.Canceled, the stream ends with codes.Unavailable and the message server is shutting down. Without that, grpc-go would end it with Canceled, and a handler that returned nil, such as a download cut short, would end its stream with OK; a handler that returns a status of its own, such as Aborted with details, keeps it; unary RPCs are not cancelled. They finish within the grace period. GracefulStop keeps each connection open until its streams have ended, so the status reaches the client, in the stream’s trailers. Unavailable is gRPC’s code for a condition the client corrects by retrying, so the end user’s client reconnects on it:
// receive is the end user's client of a subscription: it receives from // stream until the stream ends, and reports whether the client should // subscribe again. func receive(stream grpc.ServerStreamingClient[testpb.StreamingOutputCallResponse]) (bool, error) { for { _, err := stream.Recv() if status.Code(err) == codes.Unavailable { // The server is going away. Reconnect: the new stream lands on another pod. return true, nil } if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) { return false, nil // the server ended the stream with OK } if err != nil { return false, err } } } The streams are cancelled when Shutdown starts, after the drain, and not when Serve’s context is done. During the drain, a load balancer may still route a client that reconnects back to this pod.
A handler blocked in Recv A handler sees the shutdown through its context. The Service doesn’t make Recv return when that context is cancelled: that would take a goroutine for each receive, which could still be blocked in grpc-go after the handler had moved on. So a handler that is blocked in Recv, waiting for its client’s next message, sees the shutdown only when the client sends, or when Stop closes the connection at the end of the grace period, and the App then exits 1 with a *humus.GracePeriodError.
A handler that has to notice shutdown while it waits receives in a goroutine and selects on its context, as it would for any call that takes no context.
The defaults grpcserver.Main is humus.Main with grpcserver.Defaults() applied before the end user’s options, and does nothing else. Defaults is one humus.Option that sets two of humus.Main’s defaults, and leaves the Host and the telemetry Builder as humus.Main’s:
A drain of humus.DrainDelay(5 * time.Second). Kubernetes removes a terminating pod from a Service’s endpoints asynchronously, so for a while after SIGTERM, clients and load balancers still send RPCs and open connections to the pod. The Service keeps serving through the drain, so those RPCs are answered rather than refused, while the endpoint removal reaches every node. It keeps serving until Shutdown, so its Serve doesn’t return during the drain, and the drain lasts the whole 5s. A grace period of 15s, rather than humus.Main’s 20s, so that the drain fits in the same budget. It gives unary RPCs, and stream handlers ending on their contexts, time to finish once Shutdown has sent every client a GOAWAY. Streams that never end don’t use it up, since Shutdown ends them. From SIGTERM, then: the Service serves through the 5s drain; Shutdown then ends every stream and waits up to 15s for the RPCs in flight, and stops what is left; and the telemetry’s shutdown, telemetry.Settings.ShutdownTimeout, takes up to 5s more. The worst case is 25s, the budget that humus.Main keeps within Kubernetes’ default terminationGracePeriodSeconds of 30s. A service whose RPCs all finish during the drain exits 5s after SIGTERM, when the drain ends.
Overriding them The end user’s options come after Defaults, so they win. grpcserver.Main(Init, humus.WithShutdownGracePeriod(10*time.Second)) has a 10s grace period and still the 5s drain, and humus.WithDrain(nil) removes the drain.
An operator overrides both without a rebuild, with the lifecycle’s variables: HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD sets the grace period, and HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY replaces the drain with a delay of its value, whatever Defaults or an option set. Each leaves the other as it was: with HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY=1s alone, the drain is 1s and the grace period still 15s.
terminationGracePeriodSeconds When Kubernetes stops a pod, it sends the container SIGTERM, and then SIGKILL once terminationGracePeriodSeconds have passed, 30 by default. The defaults already use the 25s that leaves room for the process to exit, so a service that raises its drain or its grace period raises terminationGracePeriodSeconds with them, in the same manifest, to at least the drain, the grace period and the telemetry’s shutdown, plus a margin. Otherwise SIGKILL ends it first: its container exits 137, its OnStop functions never run, and the telemetry it had not yet exported is lost.
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: carts spec: selector: matchLabels: app: carts template: metadata: labels: app: carts spec: # 5s drain + 30s grace period + 5s telemetry shutdown, and a margin. terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45 containers: - name: carts image: registry.example.com/carts:1.0.0 ports: - name: grpc containerPort: 9090 env: - name: GRPC_ADDR value: ":9090" - name: GRPC_TLS_P12_FILE value: /etc/carts/tls/tls.p12 - name: GRPC_TLS_P12_PASSWORD valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: carts-tls key: password - name: HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD value: 30s volumeMounts: - name: tls mountPath: /etc/carts/tls readOnly: true volumes: - name: tls secret: secretName: carts-tls # tls.p12: the PKCS#12 bundle The drain does the job of a preStop hook that sleeps, which services without one add for the same reason. A pod that has both spends the hook’s sleep and the drain out of the same terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
grpcserver.Main or humus.Main Which Main a process calls depends on what a load balancer routes to, as the lifecycle’s runtime packages explains:
A process uses grpcserver.Main when a load balancer, or a Kubernetes Service, routes RPCs to its gRPC server, a gRPC service alone or one next to a job or a queue consumer. That server needs the drain, and the other Services then get its 5s drain and 15s grace period, rather than humus.Main’s 20s grace period with no drain. A process that no load balancer routes to, such as a job, calls humus.Main, with no drain. A drain would make a finished job wait for the whole delay. A process that serves HTTP and gRPC, each routed to, uses either package’s Main. Each package’s defaults set both the drain and the grace period, so passing the other package’s defaults as well replaces both: the last one wins.
Health probes Kubernetes’ gRPC probes can’t reach the Service on most clusters. A probe with grpc: connects in plain text and presents no client certificate, and the Service serves nothing in plain text. grpcserver serves no probes, and registers no health service. The module’s grpchealth package answers gRPC health v1 from an App’s health.Probes, in two ways:
grpchealth.NewService, on a plaintext port of its own, for a cluster whose grpc probes can’t use TLS, which is most clusters today. It registers only grpc.health.v1.Health, so the end user’s services are never reachable in plain text. It owns the App’s readiness, so Init returns it next to the gRPC Service and no health Service. It serves through the drain and shuts down as this Service does. grpchealth.NewServer, registered on this Service, next to a health Service, on a cluster with the GRPCContainerProbeTLS feature gate on. A probe with mode: TLS then connects over TLS, and reaches the Service on its own port, with no second one, unless the Service requires client certificates with ClientAuth: the kubelet presents none. The gate is alpha and off by default; see Kubernetes' Use TLS with gRPC probes. grpc-go’s clients reach it on every cluster, for client-side health checking. Health shows both wirings, the names they answer, the manifests and how to test them.
Telemetry The Service takes everything from the Setup’s telemetry, and never reads or sets OpenTelemetry’s globals. The first of humus’s options is a stats handler, OpenTelemetry’s gRPC instrumentation, otelgrpc, given the TracerProvider, the MeterProvider and the Propagator of s.Telemetry.
The span and the metric Each RPC gets one server span, named after the method without its leading slash, such as grpc.testing.TestService/UnaryCall. Its parent is the trace context the RPC’s metadata brought in, extracted with the Setup’s propagator, so an RPC joins its caller’s trace. The propagator comes from the telemetry Builder and decides which metadata carries the trace context: traceparent and tracestate, and baggage, with telemetry.New’s. The span carries the attributes of OpenTelemetry’s RPC semantic conventions, among them rpc.system.name, rpc.method, server.port and rpc.response.status_code.
Its status is Error for the codes that are the server’s errors: Unknown, DeadlineExceeded, Unimplemented, Internal, Unavailable and DataLoss. It is left unset for every other code, such as NotFound, which is the caller’s error rather than the server’s.
Each RPC also records the histogram rpc.server.call.duration on the Setup’s MeterProvider, in otelgrpc’s instrumentation scope.
These are the names of the stable RPC conventions, which otelgrpc uses unless OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN, read from the real environment rather than the Process’s, asks for the old ones with rpc/old or rpc/dup.
The log records The Service writes one log record of its own, for a panic, through the LoggerProvider of the Setup’s telemetry, with the logger name github.com/z5labs/humus/grpc/grpcserver:
Record Severity When RPC panicked, with rpc.method, exception.type, exception.message and exception.stacktrace, in the RPC’s context ERROR a handler or an interceptor in opts panics: see Panics The lifecycle’s own records, such as serving and shutting down, come from the App as for any Service.
Error spans at a rollout otelgrpc marks the span of each stream that Shutdown ends Error, as it does for every Unavailable. So a rollout records one error span for each stream that was open on each pod it replaced. That is accurate: the server ended those streams.
gRFC A66 metrics otelgrpc follows OpenTelemetry’s semantic conventions, which the rest of an OpenTelemetry setup and the HTTP server’s instrumentation use. An end user who also wants the metrics of gRFC A66, grpc-go’s own OpenTelemetry metrics, such as grpc.server.call.duration, passes grpc-go’s stats/opentelemetry in opts as a second stats handler, given the Setup’s MeterProvider, and grpc-go calls it after humus’s:
svc, err := grpcserver.NewService(s, settings, opentelemetry.ServerOption(opentelemetry.Options{ MetricsOptions: opentelemetry.MetricsOptions{MeterProvider: s.Telemetry.MeterProvider}, })) grpc-go’s logger grpc-go’s own logger is an ambient leak. Its grpclog package reads GRPC_GO_LOG_SEVERITY_LEVEL, GRPC_GO_LOG_VERBOSITY_LEVEL and GRPC_GO_LOG_FORMATTER, and its internal/envconfig package reads its other GRPC_* variables, from the real environment rather than the Process’s, and it writes to the real standard error, outside the App’s telemetry. It is on the lifecycle’s list of ambient leaks.
Replacing it means grpclog.SetLoggerV2, which is process-wide state, and humus sets none. An end user who wants grpc-go’s logs in their telemetry sets the logger in main, before calling grpcserver.Main, with a grpclog.LoggerV2 that writes to their telemetry. Until then, a test sees what grpc-go logs only on the test binary’s real standard error.
Panics A handler that panics fails only its own RPC. grpc-go recovers nothing, so the outermost of humus’s interceptors, a unary and a stream one, do. They run inside the stats handler and outside the end user’s interceptors, so the panic of an interceptor in opts is recovered too. The Service:
fails the RPC with codes.Internal and the message internal error, so the panic’s value never reaches the client. A stream that had already sent messages ends with that status; records the panic on the RPC’s span as an exception event, and the span’s status is Error, from the Internal code; emits one ERROR record, RPC panicked, as The log records describes, in the RPC’s context, so the record carries the span’s trace and span IDs. Every other RPC, and the server, carry on. The cost is that of net/http’s recovery: whatever the handler left half-changed stays that way. A lock it held is never released, and a structure it was updating is left as it was when it panicked, for the RPCs that come after.
Only RPCs are recovered. The lifecycle itself, the end user’s Init and the Service’s Serve and Shutdown, never recovers a panic.
Testing A gRPC service is tested whole, inside testing/synctest, as Testing a humus App describes for any App, with two functions from grpcservertest:
grpcservertest.Start is humustest.Start with grpcserver.Defaults() applied before the test’s options, and does nothing else. A test of a main that calls grpcserver.Main runs with the drain and the grace period production runs with, and can’t forget them: an RPC that never returns is cancelled 20s after SIGTERM. Options given with humustest.WithApp come after the defaults, so they win, and HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD and HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY, given with humustest.WithEnv, override them as an operator’s manifest does. grpcservertest.NewClient(t, h, address, roots) returns a *grpc.ClientConn for the Service listening on address in the test Host h. It dials through the Host, never resolves address, and verifies the Service’s certificate for address’s host against roots. A certificate from another CA, or for another name, fails the handshake, and the RPC fails with Unavailable. The client is closed when the test ends. A whole service This test runs a service whose stream would never end on the package’s defaults, with a certificate from a CA that humustest.NewCA generates for the test, so no key or certificate is ever written into the repository. serves and settingsFor are helpers of the test file: settingsFor returns Settings on :9090 with a certificate for carts from the CA, and serves returns an Init whose only Service serves the handler on them:
func TestMain_shutdown_ends_a_stream_with_Unavailable(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { ca := humustest.NewCA(t) h := humustest.NewHost(t) p, exit := grpcservertest.Start(t, serves(settingsFor(t, ca, ":9090"), subscriber{}), humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host())), ) <-h.Listening("carts:9090") client := testpb.NewTestServiceClient(grpcservertest.NewClient(t, h, "carts:9090", ca.Pool())) stream, err := client.StreamingOutputCall(t.Context(), &testpb.StreamingOutputCallRequest{}) require.NoError(t, err) _, err = stream.Recv() require.NoError(t, err) <-p.Notified(syscall.SIGTERM) begin := time.Now() p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) _, err = stream.Recv() require.Equal(t, codes.Unavailable, status.Code(err), err) require.Equal(t, "server is shutting down", status.Convert(err).Message()) require.Equal(t, 5*time.Second, time.Since(begin)) // the drain, then Shutdown ends the stream st := <-exit require.Zero(t, st.Code(), "cause: %v", st.Cause()) }) } Fake time means the drain costs the test nothing: the stream ends 5s after SIGTERM, in no real time at all.
Giving the App its certificate Start makes no CA and no certificate: how the end user’s Init sources its certificate, from which variable and in which encoding, is the end user’s decision. The test gives it one the way production does. It issues a certificate from its CA for the name it dials, writes it into the Host’s filesystem with humustest.WithFiles, and sets the variables that name the file and its password with humustest.WithEnv. For the Init that reads the PKCS#12 bundle above, the tests do it with a helper:
// p12Env returns a test Host holding a PKCS#12 bundle with a certificate // for carts from ca, as tls.p12, and the environment that names it and its // password, with addr as GRPC_ADDR. func p12Env(t *testing.T, ca *humustest.CA, addr string) (*humustest.Host, map[string]string) { t.Helper() bundle, password := ca.Issue(t, "carts").PKCS12(t) h := humustest.NewHost(t, humustest.WithFiles(map[string][]byte{"tls.p12": bundle})) return h, map[string]string{ "GRPC_ADDR": addr, "GRPC_TLS_P12_FILE": "tls.p12", "GRPC_TLS_P12_PASSWORD": password, } } and start the App with it, then call it with a client that trusts the CA:
ca := humustest.NewCA(t) h, env := p12Env(t, ca, ":9090") p, exit := grpcservertest.Start(t, Init, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host()), humus.WithTelemetry(telemetry.NoopBuilder)), humustest.WithEnv(env), ) <-h.Listening("carts:9090") client := testpb.NewTestServiceClient(grpcservertest.NewClient(t, h, "carts:9090", ca.Pool())) resp, err := client.UnaryCall(t.Context(), &testpb.SimpleRequest{}) require.NoError(t, err) require.Equal(t, "greeter", resp.GetUsername()) Each certificate has a new random key, and each bundle a new random password, so nothing secret is fixed in the test. A test that builds the grpcserver.Settings itself, as settingsFor does, sets their TLS config from cert.TLS() instead. Either way, the test passes the CA’s Pool() to NewClient.
The same Init with no environment at all checks that Addr and TLS are required:
func TestInit_without_an_address_or_a_certificate_exits_78(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { _, exit := grpcservertest.Start(t, Init) st := <-exit require.Equal(t, humus.ExitConfig, st.Code()) require.ErrorContains(t, st.Cause(), "config GRPC_ADDR: not found") require.ErrorContains(t, st.Cause(), "config GRPC_TLS_P12_FILE: not found") }) } A plaintext server Transport credentials in NewClient’s options replace its own, since they are applied after them. A test of a server that serves plain text, such as grpchealth’s probes port, passes insecure.NewCredentials(), and nil roots:
conn := grpcservertest.NewClient(t, h, "localhost:8081", nil, grpc.WithTransportCredentials(insecure.NewCredentials()), ) NewClient works without grpcservertest.Start. It needs only the Host the App runs on and the roots its certificate chains to, so it works next to an App started with humustest.Start, or with another runtime package’s Start, in a test of a process that serves gRPC next to HTTP.
The dns resolver and synctest A client’s target must not use the dns resolver. A gRPC client looks its target up with a resolver, picked by the target’s scheme. A target with no scheme, such as carts:9090, gets grpc-go’s default, the dns resolver, which looks the host up with net.DefaultResolver, whatever dialler the client has. That reaches the real network, where a name that exists only on the test Host is not found. Inside a testing/synctest bubble it is worse: the lookup crashes the test binary with fatal error: send on synctest channel from outside bubble.
So NewClient targets passthrough:/// and the address. The passthrough resolver hands the address to the dialler as it is, and the dialler is the Host’s: no lookup is made, and a name that exists nowhere but on the test Host works, inside a bubble or out. A test that builds a client of its own, with grpc.NewClient, does the same: it targets passthrough:/// and the address, and dials through the Host with grpc.WithContextDialer, whose function takes no network, so it calls h.Dial(ctx, "tcp", addr).
The Service contract grpcserver’s own tests hold the Service to the Service contract with humustest.TestService, and a Service of the end user’s own that wraps it is checked the same way:
func TestService_meets_the_Service_contract(t *testing.T) { humustest.TestService(t, func(t *testing.T, s *humus.Setup) humus.Service { cert := humustest.NewCA(t).Issue(t, "carts") svc, err := grpcserver.NewService(s, grpcserver.Settings{ Addr: ":9090", TLS: &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert.TLS()}}, }) require.NoError(t, err) testpb.RegisterTestServiceServer(svc, &testServer{}) return svc }) } The Service keeps serving after Serve’s context is done, so the subtest for Shutdown after Serve has returned on its own reports SKIP, as TestService documents. A Service built with grpc.WaitForHandlers(false) in opts fails the contract: a handler outlives Shutdown, and TestService reports its goroutine as a leak.
Migration from grpc.NewApi grpcserver replaces the grpc package from before the reset, whose grpc.NewApi built a *grpc.Server that nothing has been able to serve since #485.
Before the reset With grpcserver grpc.NewApi() grpcserver.NewService(s, settings, opts...), in the end user’s Init (*Api).RegisterService, called by generated code (*Service).RegisterService. Generated RegisterXServer(svc, impl) calls don’t change. running an Api: not possible since #485 grpcserver.Main, with the Service among the Services the end user’s Init returns internal/grpcserver’s unbounded GracefulStop Shutdown: every stream ends with Unavailable, then GracefulStop, bounded by the grace period, then Stop stats/opentelemetry fed from otel.Get* otelgrpc fed from s.Telemetry an implementation that is a health.Monitor is health-checked implicitly nothing implicit: the monitor goes in the readiness of grpchealth.NewService, or of the health Service whose Probes grpchealth.NewServer answers from internal/grpchealth grpchealth.NewServer, registered on the Service, or grpchealth.NewService on a plaintext port of its own; see Health grpc/internal/echopb in tests grpc-go’s interop/grpc_testing a handler’s panic ends the process the RPC fails with Internal, and the panic is logged

body:
humus packages are configured with plain Go values. They read no environment variables for their settings, define no variable names and read no files on your behalf; the few variables humus does read are listed below. Every value is sourced in your own Init, with whatever names and formats your service already uses: an environment variable called READ_TIMEOUT or MYSVC_HTTP_READ_TIMEOUT, a duration written 5s, a file of PEM, a flag. The usual tool is bedrock’s config package, and this page uses it throughout.
A framework that defined variable names would have to teach them, keep them consistent and document them twice. With Go values, godoc is the only documentation of a package’s settings, and a service’s variables are whatever its team chooses.
The design behind everything on this page is in the configuration revision of Proposal: configuration for humus apps.
What a package with settings exports Every humus package with settings exports the same three things:
a Settings struct, whose fields are plain values; DefaultSettings(), which returns the package’s defaults; a check function, Check<Field>, for each field that has a valid range. A zero field means zero, never “use the default”. A package’s defaults are the values DefaultSettings returns, and nothing else: a field left at zero is checked, and used, as zero. This keeps zero meaningful, as it is for net/http’s timeouts, where a zero ReadTimeout means no timeout.
The godoc of each field gives its default, its valid range and its meaning, and names its check. A check is a func(T) error. Its error says what is wrong, such as must not be negative, and does not name the field: whatever reads the value adds the name.
The samples on this page use a stand-in, declared in the root package’s tests in the shape every package gives it. The telemetry package’s Settings has the same shape, and Telemetry sources it with the same pattern, in the App’s telemetry Builder rather than in Init:
// Settings configures a Greeter. Every field is a plain value, and a field's // zero value means zero, never "use the default". type Settings struct { // Greeting is what the Greeter says. Default "hello". Greeting string // ReadTimeout bounds reading a whole request. Default 5s. Zero means // no timeout. Must not be negative; checked by CheckReadTimeout. ReadTimeout time.Duration // MaxConns is how many connections the Greeter serves at once. // Default 100. Must be positive; checked by CheckMaxConns. MaxConns int } // DefaultSettings returns the defaults of a Greeter. func DefaultSettings() Settings { return Settings{ Greeting: "hello", ReadTimeout: 5 * time.Second, MaxConns: 100, } } // CheckReadTimeout reports why d is not a valid ReadTimeout, or nil if it // is. func CheckReadTimeout(d time.Duration) error { if d < 0 { return errors.New("must not be negative") } return nil } // CheckMaxConns reports why n is not a valid MaxConns, or nil if it is. func CheckMaxConns(n int) error { if n <= 0 { return errors.New("must be positive") } return nil } In a real service these come from the package, as httpserver.Settings, httpserver.DefaultSettings() and httpserver.CheckReadTimeout, and you never copy a range out of godoc. Serving HTTP sources httpserver.Settings this way.
Sourcing Settings in Init Init reads the package’s Settings with config.Struct. Each field is one config.Value chain: where the value comes from, how it is parsed, .Default with the field of DefaultSettings(), and then the package’s check, chained with .Validate:
func GreeterInit(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { d := DefaultSettings() env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) } settings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) Settings { return Settings{ // The file is read as part of the setting, so a missing file // is a config error named after the variable. Greeting: r.Get(env("GREETING_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Default(d.Greeting)), ReadTimeout: r.Get(env("READ_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(d.ReadTimeout).Validate(CheckReadTimeout)), MaxConns: r.Get(env("MAX_CONNS").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(d.MaxConns).Validate(CheckMaxConns)), } }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78: every bad variable, one line each } g, err := NewGreeter(settings, s.Process.Stdout) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{g}, nil } The check goes after .Default, and the order matters for two reasons:
The default is checked too. A value that is not set is never checked, so a check chained before .Default would let a bad default through. Chained after it, a bad default fails exactly as a bad variable does. The error names the variable. A check in a field’s chain fails under that value’s name, so the error says READ_TIMEOUT, which is what an operator sets. A check on the whole struct could only name the field, ReadTimeout, which no operator sets. config.Struct attempts every Get, even after one has failed, so a misconfigured service reports all of its problems in one error rather than one per restart. Read every value through the Process and the Host in Setup, never through package os, so that the whole App runs in a test.
Reading a file A setting that names a file reads the file inside the field’s chain. Here GREETING_FILE is parsed by readFile, which opens the file through s.Host.FS:
// readFile returns a parser for config.Value.Parse that reads the whole // file a variable names, through fsys. func readFile(fsys humus.FS) func(name string) (string, error) { return func(name string) (string, error) { f, err := fsys.Open(name) if err != nil { return "", err } defer func() { _ = f.Close() }() b, err := io.ReadAll(f) return string(b), err } } Because the file is read as part of the setting, a missing or unreadable file is a config error named after its variable, and it exits 78 with the rest. humus.FS has no ReadFile: a helper this small is your code, not humus’s API, and it stays unexported. The same goes for decoding: a package takes a decoded value, such as a *tls.Config, never a path or a file’s contents, so how a certificate is stored and encoded is yours to decide. A further .Parse in the chain does the decoding.
How a bad value fails A bad value renders as config <variable>: <cause>. With READ_TIMEOUT=-5s and MAX_CONNS=lots, the App above logs both at ERROR through its telemetry, in one record of two lines, and exits 78:
init: config READ_TIMEOUT: must not be negative config MAX_CONNS: strconv.Atoi: parsing "lots": invalid syntax The lifecycle wraps the error Init returns once, as init: <error>, and logs it as it renders. config.Struct joins its failures with errors.Join, which renders one line per failure, so only the first line carries the init: prefix. Every line that names a bad variable starts config , prefix or not, and that is the word to search for.
And with GREETING_FILE naming a file that does not exist:
init: config GREETING_FILE: openat etc/greeter/greeting.txt: no such file or directory The cause is whatever the Host’s FS returned. This output is from the example, on a humustest Host, whose FS opens files through an os.Root, hence openat. On humus.OSHost() the same file fails with open <path>: no such file or directory.
Every error a config.Value returns is a *config.Error. When one is in the chain of the error Init returns, the App exits 78 (humus.ExitConfig, EX_CONFIG from sysexits.h), which tells an operator “fix the configuration” apart from “the service failed”. errors.AsType[*config.Error] finds the first bad variable in the chain, which is READ_TIMEOUT in the run above. A test that checks every bad variable walks the joined error, whose Unwrap() []error returns one *config.Error per variable, or compares the whole of the record the App logged. The lifecycle’s exit codes list the rest.
Building Settings in code config is a convenience, not a requirement. Settings can come from flags, a YAML file, or plain code:
settings := DefaultSettings() settings.ReadTimeout = -time.Second settings.MaxConns = 0 _, err := NewGreeter(settings, io.Discard) fmt.Println(err) A Settings built this way never passes through a check in a config chain, so the package’s constructor runs every check itself. It reports every bad field in one error, naming each field rather than a variable:
ReadTimeout: must not be negative MaxConns: must be positive The constructor of the stand-in shows the shape:
func NewGreeter(s Settings, out io.Writer) (*Greeter, error) { var errs []error if err := CheckReadTimeout(s.ReadTimeout); err != nil { errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("ReadTimeout: %w", err)) } if err := CheckMaxConns(s.MaxConns); err != nil { errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("MaxConns: %w", err)) } if err := errors.Join(errs...); err != nil { return nil, err } return &Greeter{settings: s, out: out}, nil } Its error is not a *config.Error, so an Init that returns it exits 1. A service that sources its settings with config and chains each check never reaches it: the bad value has already exited 78, named after its variable.
The variables humus reads humus reads the environment in two places, and neither is a setting of a package:
The lifecycle reads its two variables, HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD and HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY. humus.App.Run reads them before it calls Init, with defaults from App’s own fields, and checks each after its default, as on this page:
HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD defaults to the App’s ShutdownGracePeriod field: humus.Main’s 20s, or whatever an option, such as a runtime package’s defaults or humus.WithShutdownGracePeriod, or an App literal set it to. HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY, when it is set, replaces the App’s Drain, whatever that is, with humus.DrainDelay of its value, and adds a drain to an App that has none. When it is not set, the App’s Drain is the drain. The lifecycle’s settings describes them.
job reads the variables its propagator’s keys name. A job’s run joins the trace of the process that started it: job.Service extracts a trace context from the Process’s environment with the telemetry’s propagator, reading each of the propagator’s keys under the name OpenTelemetry’s environment-variable carriers give it. With telemetry.New’s propagator, those are TRACEPARENT, TRACESTATE and BAGGAGE; a Builder with a propagator of another kind, such as B3, changes them. When none is set, or the value is malformed, the run starts a new trace and nothing fails. Jobs describes them.
Apart from the lifecycle’s two, humus still defines no variable names. The names job reads are OpenTelemetry’s: its specification names them, from the propagator’s keys, so a process that starts a job sets the same variables whatever language the job is written in. The telemetry package reads no OTEL_* variable either: a Builder that wants them maps them onto telemetry.Settings itself, as Telemetry shows.
Logging and secrets humus logs no settings, and it does not redact any. Whether to log the values a service started with, which ones, and how to hide a secret among them are your decisions. Init is given the same Process and Host that humus has, so it can log anything it wants, environment variables included, to s.Process.Stderr or to a logger of its own.
What humus does log is the error Init returns, through the App’s telemetry, and a parse error often quotes the value it could not parse: parsing "lots" above. A malformed secret, such as a token in the wrong format or a key that does not decode, would be logged the same way. Keeping a secret out of that error is part of the same choice: give the secret’s chain a parser of your own whose error says what is wrong without quoting the input.
Testing it Settings are tested by running the whole App with humustest.Start: humustest.WithEnv sets the variables, and a humustest Host holds the files the settings name. One of the root package’s examples runs the App above this way:
h := humustest.NewHost(t, humustest.WithFiles(files)) tel := humustest.NewTelemetry() p, status := humustest.Start(t, GreeterInit, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host()), humus.WithTelemetry(tel.Builder())), humustest.WithEnv(env), ) st := <-status humus.WithHost replaces the Host Start builds with one the example made with its files, and humus.WithTelemetry passes humustest.Telemetry’s Builder, so the example prints the errors the App logged from the recorder’s Logs(). Both are humus’s own options, passed with humustest.WithApp as main passes them to humus.Main.
The App runs with Main’s defaults, so its grace period is Main’s 20s, as in production, and a HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD or HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY the test passes in WithEnv overrides it, as an operator’s would. WithEnv given twice keeps only the last map, so a test that adds to a base environment merges the maps itself, as Testing a humus App shows.
A relative name given to the humustest Host’s FS is relative to the test’s temp directory, and an absolute one, from h.Path, must be inside it, so a setting naming a file never reaches the real disk. Testing a humus App covers the Host in full.

A humus App builds its OpenTelemetry providers before Init, hands them to Init as one value, logs through them, and shuts them down last. The telemetry package builds them from a plain Settings value. humus.Main builds them from telemetry.DefaultSettings() unless the service passes a Builder of its own, which sources that value the same way Init sources any other package’s settings.
The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: OpenTelemetry without globals, Revision 2. The lifecycle describes when the App builds its telemetry and shuts it down.
Where the providers come from A Service gets its providers from s.Telemetry, the telemetry.SDK in the Setup that Init is given. An SDK is a plain struct: a TracerProvider, a MeterProvider, a LoggerProvider, a Propagator, and the Shutdown that the App calls once it has stopped. Neither Init nor a Service calls Shutdown.
humus never reads or sets OpenTelemetry’s global providers or its global propagator, and it never replaces slog.Default. Every humus package takes an SDK, and third-party instrumentation is handed its providers explicitly: otelhttp’s options, grpc’s stats/opentelemetry options, and otelslog.WithLoggerProvider. This Init takes its Service’s tracer and logger from s.Telemetry:
func CartsInit(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { tracer := s.Telemetry.TracerProvider.Tracer("carts") logger := otelslog.NewLogger("carts", otelslog.WithLoggerProvider(s.Telemetry.LoggerProvider)) return []humus.Service{&cartJob{tracer: tracer, logger: logger}}, nil } A library that reads only the global providers can be given them: set them in Init, from s.Telemetry. That is your decision and your global state, not humus’s. The one piece of global state humus does set is OpenTelemetry’s error handler.
Main’s default App.Telemetry is a telemetry.Builder. humus.Main defaults it to one that calls telemetry.New with telemetry.DefaultSettings(), the Host’s Dial and the Process’s stdout. So a service that passes no Builder:
writes its log records to standard output, as JSON lines in the console log format; gives its spans real trace and span IDs, which its log records carry, and exports none; builds no exporter that dials out, so it needs no collector, and a service that forgets its Builder doesn’t fail. The defaults below describe what DefaultSettings() does in full. humustest.Start keeps the same default, so a whole-App test that passes no Builder sees on p.Stdout() the JSON lines production would write. This example runs the App of this page that way:
p, status := humustest.Start(t, CartsInit) st := <-status printConsoleLogs(p.Stdout(), "carts") fmt.Println("exit code:", st.Code()) // Output: // INFO "cart created" map[cart.id:c-123], trace context: true // INFO "cart created, untraced" map[], trace context: false // exit code: 0 A service that exports anything passes its own Builder, with humus.WithTelemetry, and so does one that names itself, since DefaultSettings() names every service unknown_service:
humus.Main(CartsInit, humus.WithTelemetry(buildCartsTelemetry)) Writing the Builder The end user’s Builder is given the context a signal cancels, the bedrock.Process and the Host’s Dial, and it does three things:
sources telemetry.Settings from p.Environment with config.Struct, starting from telemetry.DefaultSettings(); chains each field’s check after its default, so a bad default fails as a bad variable does, and the error names the variable; calls telemetry.New with the Settings, dial and p.Stdout. Configuring a humus service explains the pattern. This Builder keeps the OpenTelemetry specification’s variable names, but the names are yours to choose:
func buildCartsTelemetry(ctx context.Context, p bedrock.Process, dial telemetry.Dialer) (telemetry.SDK, error) { d := telemetry.DefaultSettings() env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(p.Environment, name) } exporter := func(name string, def telemetry.Exporter) config.Value[telemetry.Exporter] { return env(name). Map(func(s string) telemetry.Exporter { return telemetry.Exporter(s) }). Default(def). Validate(telemetry.CheckExporter) } s, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) telemetry.Settings { s := d s.Disabled = r.Get(env("OTEL_SDK_DISABLED").Parse(strconv.ParseBool).Default(d.Disabled)) s.ServiceName = r.Get(env("OTEL_SERVICE_NAME").Default("carts").Validate(telemetry.CheckServiceName)) s.Traces = r.Get(exporter("OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER", d.Traces)) s.Metrics = r.Get(exporter("OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER", d.Metrics)) s.Logs = r.Get(exporter("OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER", d.Logs)) return s }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return telemetry.SDK{}, err // exit 78: every bad variable, one line each } return telemetry.New(ctx, s, dial, p.Stdout) } s := d starts from every default, so a field the Builder does not source, such as LogLevel here, keeps its default. DefaultSettings cannot see the process, so it names the service unknown_service. The Builder names it.
With OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=zipkin, this App never calls Init. It writes the error to standard error, because it has no telemetry yet to log it through, and exits 78:
build telemetry: config OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER: "zipkin" is not one of none, console or otlp telemetry.New runs every check too, so a Settings built in code is checked as well. Its error names each bad field, such as telemetry: Settings.Traces: "zipkin" is not one of none, console or otlp, and an App whose Builder returns it exits 1, not 78: the bad value came from code, not from a variable.
A Builder that needs something Settings does not cover, such as a metric view or a Prometheus reader, builds the SDK value itself, Shutdown included. humustest’s recorder is built that way.
Settings telemetry.Settings follows the shape every humus package’s settings take: plain values, DefaultSettings(), and a check for each field with a valid range. A zero field means zero, never “use the default”.
Field Default Valid Check Spec variable Disabled false any OTEL_SDK_DISABLED ServiceName "unknown_service" not empty CheckServiceName OTEL_SERVICE_NAME ResourceOptions none, so no detector runs any OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, as resource.WithAttributes Traces ExporterNone none, console, otlp CheckExporter OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER Metrics ExporterNone none, console, otlp CheckExporter OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER Logs ExporterConsole none, console, otlp CheckExporter OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER OTLP.Endpoint "localhost:4317" host:port, with a port from 1 to 65535 CheckOTLPEndpoint OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, which is a URL in the spec OTLP.Protocol ProtocolGRPC grpc, http/protobuf CheckOTLPProtocol OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL OTLP.Headers none any OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS OTLP.TLS nil, which means plaintext any OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_CERTIFICATE and the related variables OTLP.Timeout 10s positive CheckOTLPTimeout OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT Sampler sdktrace.ParentBased(sdktrace.AlwaysSample()) not nil CheckSampler OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER and OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG LogLevel log.SeverityInfo log.SeverityTrace1 to log.SeverityFatal4 CheckLogLevel none ShutdownTimeout 5s positive CheckShutdownTimeout none The godoc of each field is the reference; the table is its summary. The OTLP fields are checked even when no signal is exported over OTLP. The OTLP exporters dial the collector through the Dialer the Builder is given, which is the Host’s Dial, and over http/protobuf each signal is sent to its spec path: /v1/traces, /v1/metrics and /v1/logs.
humus reads none of these variables. The last column names the specification’s variable with the same meaning, for a Builder that wants to stay compatible with it, as the one above does. It is not a variable humus reads: there is no FromEnvironment and no parser for the specification’s formats. So a platform that injects OTEL_* variables, such as the OpenTelemetry Operator, has no effect on an App unless its Builder reads them.
telemetry.New gives the OpenTelemetry SDK every option explicitly, at the SDK’s own default where Settings has no field, so the SDK’s own reads of the real environment are overridden too. The few that still take effect, such as OTEL_GO_X_*, are listed under the lifecycle’s ambient leaks.
The defaults With DefaultSettings():
Logs are written to standard output, as one line of JSON per record, in the console log format. Traces are not exported, but spans still get IDs. At ExporterNone, the TracerProvider is still the SDK’s, built with the Sampler and the resource but with no span processor. Every span gets a real trace ID and span ID, and a record logged in it carries them, but nothing is exported. That is the usual local setup: the logs on standard output can be grouped by request without running a collector. Metrics are a no-op. Sampling is the same with or without an exporter: the TracerProvider keeps the configured Sampler, so the sampled flag passed on to downstream services does not change when Traces does.
Traces at none have a cost in the middle of a shared trace. A service at none in a traced call chain passes on span IDs that no backend ever receives. The trace ID is still the caller’s, so the trace holds together, but the downstream spans point to a parent that is missing. A service that takes part in a traced system sets Traces to otlp.
The console log format At ExporterConsole, each log record is written to standard output as one line of JSON, terminated by a newline:
{"timestamp":"2026-10-16T06:56:32.447829601Z","severity_text":"INFO","severity_number":9,"body":"cart created","trace_id":"e2f668b6c06f2de82e61e2517c2d7a07","span_id":"ff25eb972a5557d5","trace_flags":"01","scope":"carts","attributes":{"cart.id":"c-123"}} This format is part of humus’s API. Renaming, reordering, adding or removing a key, or encoding a value differently, is a breaking change. It is humus’s own, written by an exporter of the telemetry package, so upgrading OpenTelemetry does not change it. A golden test pins it byte for byte.
The keys are always written in this order, and each one only when the record has what it holds:
Key Value Present timestamp the record’s timestamp or, when that is unset, its observed timestamp, in UTC, as RFC 3339 with exactly nine fractional digits always severity_text the record’s severity text or, when that is empty, the short name of its severity number: TRACE, TRACE2, …, INFO, …, FATAL4 when the severity number is set, that is when it is one of OpenTelemetry’s severities 1 to 24 severity_number the record’s OpenTelemetry severity number, 1 to 24, for filtering by threshold under the same condition as severity_text event_name the record’s event name when it is not empty body the record’s body, encoded as below when the body is set trace_id, span_id, trace_flags the trace context of the span the record was logged in, as lowercase hex: 32, 16 and 2 digits only when the record has a valid span context, one whose trace ID and span ID are both non-zero scope the name of the record’s instrumentation scope, the name its logger was created with always, and empty when that name is attributes an object whose keys are the attribute keys, in the record’s order when the record has at least one attribute The keys are the OpenTelemetry log data model’s field names, in snake case. The trace context keys follow OpenTelemetry’s stable specification for trace context in non-OTLP log formats, so a log pipeline links a line to its trace by the names the specification gives. A record logged outside a span has none of the three, rather than zeros, because a zero ID would point to a trace that does not exist.
The record’s resource is never written: OTLP carries the resource, and on standard output whatever collects the logs, such as a Kubernetes log agent, adds its own metadata. Neither is its count of dropped attributes.
A body and an attribute value are encoded the same way:
a string as a JSON string, a bool as true or false, and an integer as a JSON number; a finite float as a JSON number, and NaN and the infinities as the strings "NaN", "+Inf" and "-Inf", so that every line is valid JSON; bytes as a string holding their standard, padded base64 encoding; a slice, typed slices included, as an array, and a map as an object with its keys sorted by their bytes, each element encoded by these rules; an empty value as null, as an attribute’s value or inside a slice or map. An empty body is not written at all. An attribute key a record holds more than once, which happens only when its logger provider allows duplicate keys, is written once for each value, and so is a key a map holds more than once. Strings are escaped as JSON requires and no further: <, > and & are written as they are. Invalid UTF-8 is replaced by U+FFFD.
The telemetry package doc is the specification of the format, and this section its summary.
Traces and metrics at ExporterConsole are written by OpenTelemetry’s stdouttrace and stdoutmetric. They are for debugging, and humus makes no promise about their format.
Trace context in logs telemetry.SDK exposes a LoggerProvider, not a logger: humus has no logging bridge of its own. Use the OpenTelemetry Logs API directly, or bridge the LoggerProvider to the logging library you already use, such as otelslog for log/slog, as CartsInit above does.
A record carries a trace context only when the log call is given the span’s context. With otelslog, that means InfoContext, not Info: Info logs with context.Background(), so its record has no trace fields, whatever exporter it goes to. In a handler, pass the request’s context, r.Context(). This Service logs both ways inside one span:
func (j *cartJob) Serve(ctx context.Context) error { ctx, span := j.tracer.Start(ctx, "create cart") defer span.End() // InfoContext, not Info: the record takes its trace context from ctx, // so it carries the span's trace_id and span_id. j.logger.InfoContext(ctx, "cart created", slog.String("cart.id", "c-123")) // Info logs with context.Background(), so this record has no trace // context, even though it is logged inside the span. j.logger.Info("cart created, untraced") return nil } With the defaults, the first line on standard output has trace_id, span_id and trace_flags, and the second has none of them.
A job’s parent trace A job’s run joins the trace of the process that started it. job.Service extracts a trace context from the Process’s environment through the SDK’s Propagator, the one s.Telemetry carries, and the run’s span is that context’s child. With telemetry.New’s propagator, W3C trace context and baggage, it reads TRACEPARENT, TRACESTATE and BAGGAGE, the names OpenTelemetry’s environment-variable carriers give its keys. A Builder whose SDK has a propagator of another kind changes the variables read along with it. When none is set, as under Kubernetes, the run starts a new trace.
These are trace context, not settings: the OTEL_* variables in the table above are still read only by a Builder that maps them. Jobs covers the run’s span in full.
Other settings LogLevel is the lowest severity the LoggerProvider exports, as an OpenTelemetry severity rather than a slog.Level. It is applied in the provider: its loggers’ Enabled reports false below it, so a bridge that asks Enabled before building a record, as otelslog’s handler does, skips a filtered record at no cost, and a record below it is dropped either way. A record with no severity, log.SeverityUndefined, is not on the scale and is kept. ShutdownTimeout bounds SDK.Shutdown: every provider is flushed and stopped within it. The App shuts telemetry down after the OnStop functions, separately from the grace period and with a context that a cancelled root context does not cancel, so ShutdownTimeout is what bounds it. Disabled is the counterpart of OTEL_SDK_DISABLED. telemetry.New ignores every other field and returns telemetry.Noop(), building and dialling nothing. The propagator stays W3C trace context plus baggage, because the specification disables signals, not propagation, so a request’s trace passes through. Unlike traces at none, a disabled SDK makes no IDs of its own: it passes on the span context a request brought. Resource detectors are opt-in. The resource is ServiceName plus whatever ResourceOptions adds, and by default no detector runs, so the resource is service.name alone. A detector, such as resource.WithHost() or a contrib cloud detector, reads the real host rather than the humus.Host: the host, process and container detectors read /etc, /proc and cgroups, and a cloud detector dials its metadata server. Opt in knowingly. ServiceName wins over a service.name any detector finds. telemetry.New fails if any option fails, even partly, and some detectors fail where their attribute cannot be found: resource.WithProcess includes the process owner, which cannot be looked up in an image without a passwd entry for its user. Opt in to the detectors whose attributes the environment has, such as resource.WithProcessPID, rather than to a group of them. Testing A test that asserts on what an App emits runs it with humustest.Start, and passes humustest.NewTelemetry()’s Builder with humustest.WithApp(humus.WithTelemetry(…)), in place of the one production uses. The recorder uses the real OpenTelemetry SDK with in-memory exporters, records every severity, samples every span, starts no goroutine, so it works under synctest, and keeps what it recorded after the App has shut it down:
tel := humustest.NewTelemetry() _, status := humustest.Start(t, CartsInit, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithTelemetry(tel.Builder())), ) st := <-status Once the App has exited, tel.Spans(), tel.Metrics(ctx) and tel.Logs() return what it emitted. Here they show the span create cart, and that the record logged with InfoContext is in it:
span := tel.Spans()[0] fmt.Println("span:", span.Name()) for _, r := range tel.Logs() { if r.InstrumentationScope().Name != "carts" { continue // the lifecycle's own records } inSpan := r.TraceID() == span.SpanContext().TraceID() && r.SpanID() == span.SpanContext().SpanID() fmt.Printf("logged %s: %s, in the span: %t\n", r.SeverityText(), r.Body().AsString(), inSpan) } The lifecycle’s own records, serving, shutting down, stopped and every failure after the telemetry is built, are in tel.Logs() too, under the scope github.com/z5labs/humus.
A test that does not assert on telemetry keeps Main’s default, or passes telemetry.NoopBuilder, whose SDK discards everything. A test of the Builder itself passes it with humustest.WithApp(humus.WithTelemetry(…)), sets the environment it reads with humustest.WithEnv, and reads standard output, where the console logs go, and standard error, where a bad variable goes. The root package’s examples run the Builder above that way.
Testing a humus App covers the rest of a whole-App test.
The error handler Telemetry cannot report its own failure: a failing OTLP log exporter would swallow the errors about itself, and each error would queue another record bound to fail. So once the SDK is built, Run sets OpenTelemetry’s process-wide error handler to one that writes each export error to the Process’s standard error, as one line starting with telemetry: . Export errors join the failures standard error already gets, those that come before there is any telemetry or that are about telemetry itself: a failure to build or shut it down, and a malformed lifecycle setting.
This is the one piece of OpenTelemetry’s global state humus sets, and its one call to otel.SetErrorHandler. Being process-wide, it has two consequences:
In a process that runs several Apps, the last App to start gets every App’s export errors. So a test that asserts on export errors does not run in parallel with another App. An end user who wants a different handler sets it in Init, which runs after Run has set its own. OpenTelemetry’s internal logger is separate from the handler, and writes its own errors to the real standard error. It is on the lifecycle’s list of ambient leaks.
